articles.title: Uzbekistan’s Death Penalty Debate Returns After Child Abuse Case
articles.full_text:
The debate over the death penalty is back in Uzbekistan, this time involving the country’s most senior officials.
For the second time in the  span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter.  
Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times. 
What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved. 
Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27. 
“We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added. 
Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements. 
“The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement. 
This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote.
Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway.
In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.” 
Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book.
Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law. 
“Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.”
Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices. 
“If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov.
While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or  low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move. 
As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control. Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation.
Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too. 
The staff of the kindergarten  who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.”
Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages. 
Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse.
“We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated.
From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. But it wasn’t until the current furor, when it became politically expedient to take action, that the legislature actually moved.
The Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis passed the bill on September 29.

articles.title: Living Under a Lethal Sky: Myanmar’s Rakhine on Edge as Military Airstrikes on Civilians Grow
articles.full_text:
Airstrikes are no longer intermittent dangers as they were two years ago, but a constant hazard. They are part of the people’s daily lives, woven into their collective consciousness.
Residents of Yoe Ngu village in Myanmar’s Rakhine State search for bodies of their kin a day after an airstrike on the village, on Feb. 24, 2026.
The stench of burnt flesh and bones was nauseating even from a distance. Mutilated and burnt body parts lay strewn amid the ruins of bombed houses. Smoke billowed from what was once a thriving market selling a wide range of commodities and catering to the needs of three villages in the area.
When I arrived at the bombed site at Yoe Ngu village in Ponnagyun township of Myanmar’s Rakhine State at 7.30 p.m. on February 24, the atmosphere was unnerving. Aside from a small group of six men holding blazing torches and using sticks and shovels to rummage through the ash and charred heaps, the village was deserted.
The men were assembling the corpses and severed limbs at a spot on a road adjacent to the market. A man sprinkled water from a bucket where the fire was yet to be extinguished. Two women who had lost their relatives sat at a far corner of the market and wept uncontrollably.
“Let’s resume our work in the morning,” an elderly man shouted. “We will not be able to extricate anything more in the dark.” Bodies and body parts were loaded onto a handcart to be taken to the cemetery for burial.
Between 2 and 2:15 p.m. that day, the Myanmar military dropped two 500-pound bombs on a market in Yoe Ngu village. Some 17 people were killed on the spot and another 15 were injured. Among the dead were a 6-year-old girl, two teenagers, four women, and an unidentified charred body.
The injured were taken to the hospital in Mrauk U, located about 80 kilometers north of the village.  Among them were eight critical cases, including a 5-year-old girl, who survived but had her right leg amputated.  A middle-aged poultry farmer succumbed to injuries two days later.
There were only about a dozen people gathering the dead bodies or searching for their missing relatives at the bombed site. All the residents had relocated to different places within a radius of 1-2 km from the village, while many of them pitched tents in the open fields. They were terrified that more airstrikes would happen that night.
Nineteen families had erected makeshift thatches of bamboo and tarpaulin in the paddy fields about a hundred meters from the highway on the northern flank of the village. Among them were 32 internally displaced persons (IDPs) from Sittwe, who were compelled to leave their villages early last year after continuous shelling by the military. They assumed they were safe in Yoe Ngu but were mistaken.
“We are back to the situation when we had to flee for our lives from Sittwe last year,” said Hla Thein Tun, whose sister died instantly after multiple splinters hit her head. “We don’t know for how long we can stay here.”
Another male IDP from Kyaukphyu was killed in the market and two sustained minor injuries.  They were among the 850-odd IDPs residing in the village with a population of about 2,500.
Until they can return to the village, the people must survive in the fields. They have to fetch food, water, and other essentials from the village. The misery is more for the elderly, children, and especially the sick people requiring greater attention and care.
“The saving grace is the ongoing winter season. The fields are dry and so there is less chance of us contracting diseases,” Than Tun, who was sitting outside the thatch in the fields with his seven family members, told me. “But then there might be airstrikes here as well.”
His fears were not misplaced. There was an aerial attack again about a mile from Yoe Ngu village on July 27, near an IDP camp, where a teenage girl sustained minor injuries.
Military’s Rationale For Increased Airstrikes 
Major Myint Zaw Than, who defected from the military last year, told The Diplomat on February 25 in Rakhine State that airstrikes on the civilian population would increase in Rakhine’s liberated region in the coming months. The rationale for the escalation was the military’s need to defend the three townships of Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and Manaung that are still under its control, he explained. The rest of the 14 townships have been overtaken by the Arakan Army (AA).
Myint Zaw Than said that after the coup in 2021, when the resistance to the junta grew, the military upgraded its capabilities. “It uses suicide drones extensively now, which was absent five years ago. Surveillance has also improved,” he said.
Winning territory lost to the AA  has been among the top priorities of the military over the past year.
Earlier, while combating the ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) in other regions, the military had resorted to airstrikes to support ground offensives. Currently, in Rakhine and other regions that are largely under the control of the EAOs, aerial attacks are being used as a separate strategy.
Some academics and journalists in Rakhine State opine that airpower is being used to weaken the armed resistance, to impose sustained pressure on the civilian populace and to wrest political concessions. They fear that after the military launched its major multi-front counteroffensive codenamed Operation 4926 on September 4, spanning several townships in Rakhine and the contiguous regions of Magway and Ayeyarwady, more airstrikes could be expected.
According to a United Nations report, airstrikes were the leading cause of civilian casualties in Myanmar in 2025, with at least 982 deaths, including 232 children.  This was a 52 percent increase compared with casualties in 2024.
Figures from ISP-Myanmar’s Conflict & Security Tracker 2026 indicate that there were at least 222 aerial attacks in Rakhine between March 31 and August 31 this year, out of a total of 1,583 air strikes across the country. Magway was the worst hit with 322 strikes.
That airstrikes against civilians are escalating have also been noted by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), which says that the increase is the result of the “tactics” employed by new military chief Ye Win Oo, who assumed charge in March, after which the military command was reconfigured.
A renewed offensive has begun in several border regions, including a frontier zone with rare earth deposits and vital trade arteries.  ACLED also said that as part of the new strategy, the military was regularly deploying “specialized groups of two to five jet fighters” hitting the same target repeatedly,
ACLED’s findings have been echoed in a report by the U.N.-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), which mentions the increasing use of low-cost aircraft such as motorized paragliders and gyrocopters in the attacks. The U.N. agency pointed out that civilian casualties are aggravated by the military’s growing use of “double-tap” aerial attacks in which a second strike follows the first, apparently “targeting first responders, people helping the wounded, and those trying to flee.”
Commenting on the increasing airstrikes, AA chief Twan Mrat Naing observed in an interview to The Diplomat on March 2 that “The military government wants to talk from a position of strength. But we will not succumb to such pressure.”
Among the worst airstrikes on civilians in Rakhine State was the attack on Mrauk U Division Hospital on December 10, 2025, which killed 33 people and left 80 injured, including seven staff members. It was a 250-bed hospital, but only 140 patients were in the hospital at the time of the attack.
Among the injured staff members was Soe Naing Tun, who was at the entrance of an adjacent building and preparing to leave for home after completing his duties at the hospital. He witnessed the shells exploding and the ensuing sequence of events in the hospital.
“Both the strikes happened at 9:15 p.m. within seconds of each other. The first strike fell on the room adjacent to the verandah where all the patients were killed. Fortunately, the second hit the field in front.  For a few seconds, it seemed as if a volcano had erupted in the main building with a deafening roar,” Soe Naing Tun recalled. He added that most of the patients who either died or were injured hailed from the townships of Ponnagyun, Kyauktaw, and Mrauk U.
articles.summary: Airstrikes are no longer intermittent dangers as they were two years ago, but a constant hazard. They are part of the people’s daily lives, woven into their collective consciousness.

articles.title: Why Are China and Japan Still So Focused on the ‘Enemy State Clauses’ of the UN Charter?
articles.full_text:
The UNGA voted to delete those sections 20 years ago. But the issue has acquired renewed political significance as Sino-Japanese relations have deteriorated.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae address the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
On September 22, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae addressed the United Nations General Assembly. She argued that Japan has become deeply embedded in the postwar international order over the past 70 years and has made significant contributions to it. Japan, she maintained, should no longer be constrained by the so-called “enemy state clauses” in the United Nations Charter. She therefore renewed Japan’s call for the U.N. to initiate the process of removing them. 
The so-called “enemy state clauses” are mainly contained in Articles 53, 77, and 107 of the U.N. Charter. They preserve special provisions concerning states that were enemies of the charter’s signatories during World War II. For Japan, these provisions have long been seen as a lingering reminder of its status as a defeated Axis power.
Japan’s call is not new. In 1995, the U.N. General Assembly adopted Resolution 50/52 with 155 votes in favor (China included), zero against and three abstentions, expressing its intention to initiate the procedure under Article 108 of the charter to delete the “enemy state clauses.” Ten years later, the 2005 World Summit Outcome, which was adopted without a vote, again declared that the references to “enemy states clauses” should be deleted. Yet the process subsequently stalled, and the charter itself has never been formally amended to remove the provisions.
In other words, the “enemy state clauses” have been widely regarded as obsolete, and the international community has repeatedly expressed its intention to remove them. Yet they remain formally embedded in the U.N. Charter. Some international lawyers therefore regard them as effectively obsolete or inoperative, while others maintain that their continued presence in the charter cannot simply be ignored. 
The issue has acquired renewed political significance as Sino-Japanese relations have deteriorated. Chinese officials have linked the clauses to Japan’s historical responsibility and its current security policies, while Tokyo maintains that the provisions are outdated and inconsistent with Japan’s position in the international community.
There is also a practical obstacle. Amending the U.N. Charter is subject to a particularly demanding procedure. Under Article 108, an amendment must be adopted by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and ratified by two-thirds of U.N. members in accordance with their respective constitutional procedures, including all permanent members of the Security Council. This means that any formal amendment cannot bypass the permanent members of the Security Council, including China and Russia. In practical terms, therefore, the removal of the clauses would require a degree of political consensus that has so far proved elusive.
The political meaning of the clauses may therefore be more important than the words themselves. To understand the dispute, it is useful to recall the historical context in which the U.N. Charter was created. The charter reflected the international order that emerged from World War II and the victorious powers’ vision of how future international security should be organized. Its provisions concerning the former enemy states were designed in the context of preventing defeated powers such as Germany and Japan from again disrupting the new security order. 
Japan, meanwhile, returned to the international community after accepting the postwar settlement and has since become an important contributor to the U.N. system. Over the decades, it has participated extensively in peacekeeping, development assistance and international organizations. So, can the “enemy state clauses” therefore still be considered appropriate today? Should contemporary Japan continue to bear restrictions that originated in the actions of a previous generation? 
China clearly believes Japan still has work to do in this regard. In response to Takaichi’s remarks, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun argued that what Japan does matters more than what it says. He linked the issue to Japan’s understanding of its wartime aggression, its current defense policies, and the stability of the postwar international order. China maintains that the “enemy state clauses” continue to have relevance as institutional safeguards against the resurgence of fascism and militarism.
For Japan, however, the removal of the clauses may represent more than the elimination of an obsolete legal provision. It may also symbolize international recognition of Japan’s transformation from a defeated power into a “normal” member of the international community – and, more broadly, its effort to move beyond aspects of the postwar system. This becomes particularly significant when viewed alongside Takaichi’s call for reform of the U.N. Security Council. In the same speech, she argued that the UNSC’s current structure still reflects the international situation of 1945 and called for an expansion of both permanent and non-permanent membership.
The dispute over the “enemy state clauses,” therefore, is not simply a disagreement over whether an outdated provision should be deleted. It reflects two different understandings of the postwar international order. From Japan’s perspective, the central question is whether the international institutional framework should continue to reflect the geopolitical realities of 1945, or whether it should recognize the country Japan has become over the past eight decades. 
From China’s perspective, however, the postwar order is not merely a set of outdated institutional arrangements. It also embodies historical memory and political understandings concerning Japan’s wartime conduct and its subsequent role in Asia. This is why the “enemy state clauses” remain politically significant even though their practical application has long been regarded as highly unlikely.
The controversy between China and Japan over the clauses therefore reveals a broader disagreement about the meaning of the postwar order. Even if Japan succeeds in removing the relevant language from the charter, the broader question of how Japan’s postwar identity is understood in Asia will not disappear with it. If Tokyo wants the “enemy state clauses” to become irrelevant not merely in legal terms but also in political terms, persuading U.N. members that the provisions are obsolete will not be enough. Japan will also need to convince its Asian neighbors, particularly those that experienced Japanese aggression, that the historical and political foundations of the postwar order can be reconciled with Japan’s evolving international role.
That is unlikely to happen overnight. The “enemy state clauses” may be remnants of a bygone era, but the debate surrounding them remains an important reflection of the unresolved political differences between China and Japan over history, identity, and the postwar international order.
On September 22, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae addressed the United Nations General Assembly. She argued that Japan has become deeply embedded in the postwar international order over the past 70 years and has made significant contributions to it. Japan, she maintained, should no longer be constrained by the so-called “enemy state clauses” in the United Nations Charter. She therefore renewed Japan’s call for the U.N. to initiate the process of removing them. 
The so-called “enemy state clauses” are mainly contained in Articles 53, 77, and 107 of the U.N. Charter. They preserve special provisions concerning states that were enemies of the charter’s signatories during World War II. For Japan, these provisions have long been seen as a lingering reminder of its status as a defeated Axis power.
Japan’s call is not new. In 1995, the U.N. General Assembly adopted Resolution 50/52 with 155 votes in favor (China included), zero against and three abstentions, expressing its intention to initiate the procedure under Article 108 of the charter to delete the “enemy state clauses.” Ten years later, the 2005 World Summit Outcome, which was adopted without a vote, again declared that the references to “enemy states clauses” should be deleted. Yet the process subsequently stalled, and the charter itself has never been formally amended to remove the provisions.
In other words, the “enemy state clauses” have been widely regarded as obsolete, and the international community has repeatedly expressed its intention to remove them. Yet they remain formally embedded in the U.N. Charter. Some international lawyers therefore regard them as effectively obsolete or inoperative, while others maintain that their continued presence in the charter cannot simply be ignored. 
The issue has acquired renewed political significance as Sino-Japanese relations have deteriorated. Chinese officials have linked the clauses to Japan’s historical responsibility and its current security policies, while Tokyo maintains that the provisions are outdated and inconsistent with Japan’s position in the international community.
There is also a practical obstacle. Amending the U.N. Charter is subject to a particularly demanding procedure. Under Article 108, an amendment must be adopted by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and ratified by two-thirds of U.N. members in accordance with their respective constitutional procedures, including all permanent members of the Security Council. This means that any formal amendment cannot bypass the permanent members of the Security Council, including China and Russia. In practical terms, therefore, the removal of the clauses would require a degree of political consensus that has so far proved elusive.
The political meaning of the clauses may therefore be more important than the words themselves. To understand the dispute, it is useful to recall the historical context in which the U.N. Charter was created. The charter reflected the international order that emerged from World War II and the victorious powers’ vision of how future international security should be organized. Its provisions concerning the former enemy states were designed in the context of preventing defeated powers such as Germany and Japan from again disrupting the new security order. 
Japan, meanwhile, returned to the international community after accepting the postwar settlement and has since become an important contributor to the U.N. system. Over the decades, it has participated extensively in peacekeeping, development assistance and international organizations. So, can the “enemy state clauses” therefore still be considered appropriate today? Should contemporary Japan continue to bear restrictions that originated in the actions of a previous generation? 
China clearly believes Japan still has work to do in this regard. In response to Takaichi’s remarks, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun argued that what Japan does matters more than what it says. He linked the issue to Japan’s understanding of its wartime aggression, its current defense policies, and the stability of the postwar international order. China maintains that the “enemy state clauses” continue to have relevance as institutional safeguards against the resurgence of fascism and militarism.
For Japan, however, the removal of the clauses may represent more than the elimination of an obsolete legal provision. It may also symbolize international recognition of Japan’s transformation from a defeated power into a “normal” member of the international community – and, more broadly, its effort to move beyond aspects of the postwar system. This becomes particularly significant when viewed alongside Takaichi’s call for reform of the U.N. Security Council. In the same speech, she argued that the UNSC’s current structure still reflects the international situation of 1945 and called for an expansion of both permanent and non-permanent membership.
The dispute over the “enemy state clauses,” therefore, is not simply a disagreement over whether an outdated provision should be deleted. It reflects two different understandings of the postwar international order. From Japan’s perspective, the central question is whether the international institutional framework should continue to reflect the geopolitical realities of 1945, or whether it should recognize the country Japan has become over the past eight decades. 
From China’s perspective, however, the postwar order is not merely a set of outdated institutional arrangements. It also embodies historical memory and political understandings concerning Japan’s wartime conduct and its subsequent role in Asia. This is why the “enemy state clauses” remain politically significant even though their practical application has long been regarded as highly unlikely.
The controversy between China and Japan over the clauses therefore reveals a broader disagreement about the meaning of the postwar order. Even if Japan succeeds in removing the relevant language from the charter, the broader question of how Japan’s postwar identity is understood in Asia will not disappear with it. If Tokyo wants the “enemy state clauses” to become irrelevant not merely in legal terms but also in political terms, persuading U.N. members that the provisions are obsolete will not be enough. Japan will also need to convince its Asian neighbors, particularly those that experienced Japanese aggression, that the historical and political foundations of the postwar order can be reconciled with Japan’s evolving international role.
That is unlikely to happen overnight. The “enemy state clauses” may be remnants of a bygone era, but the debate surrounding them remains an important reflection of the unresolved political differences between China and Japan over history, identity, and the postwar international order.

articles.title: Taiwan Should Be Kept Off the Negotiating Table
articles.full_text:
The fact that Trump didn’t give anything new away on Taiwan shouldn’t obscure how much ground he has already conceded to Xi.
U.S. President Trump delivers remarks to the press ahead of a summit meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
The much-heralded China-U.S. summit is now behind us, and the consensus is that it produced nothing of substance. President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extended their trade truce, talked about artificial intelligence, and agreed on little else. 
Many have applied the same measure to Taiwan: Xi pressed Trump to shift American policy on the island, the American leader appears not to have obliged, and so, the reasoning goes, the U.S. position held and nothing happened. That reading is wrong. What looks like nothing is the clearest sign yet of how far the U.S. position on Taiwan has shifted. And Trump is solely responsible for such a change.
Consider how the island came to be on the negotiating table in the first place: Trump placed it there. Back in February he told reporters he was discussing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan with Xi, something no president had done since 1982, when President Ronald Reagan promised Taipei that Washington would not consult Beijing on such matters. In May, in an interview taped just after the Beijing summit, Trump called a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan a “negotiating chip.” Then, on his flight home, he confirmed that he and Xi had again discussed the sales. Reminded of Reagan’s commitment, Trump dismissed it as ancient history. The package, ready for his signature since March, is still unsigned. 
Each of these points marked a unilateral concession on Taiwan, made without receiving anything durable in return. 
Trump went into the summit last week needing an agreement with Xi even more than he had in the spring. Inflation had risen, the war with Iran had dragged on, and his approval stood at or near the lows of his presidency weeks before the midterms. A meeting that produced a “win” of any kind would have allowed him to claim a much sought after victory. The concern was that he would further sacrifice Taiwan to achieve it.
That he appears not to have taken this route, while not to be overlooked, is almost beside the point. Before the curtains rose on the Trump-Xi summit, Trump had already moved the U.S. position on Taiwan toward China, and as a result Xi arrived in a position where he simply could not lose. Had Trump conceded further, it would have been a ground-changing win for China. When Trump instead lavished praise on his guest and declined to give more, it was still a win, only a quieter one: Beijing banked the new status quo, the one Trump created this year, in which merely holding the line counts as U.S. firmness.
Such a prospect is compounded by two further issues. First, it is not known what Trump said to Xi in private; public silence is reassuring only if it matches what passed behind closed doors. And just after the summit, he did little to quell concerns on this score. Instead, on his way to a college football game, he responded enigmatically to a question about Taiwan: “We didn’t talk about it too much.” He added, “Right now, it’s fine. It’s just moving along,” and then, referring specifically to Xi, Trump said: “He understands very much how I feel.” His comments served to suggest that some private understanding with Xi on Taiwan has been reached but not disclosed. 
Second, Trump has confirmed that he and Xi will meet twice more before the year is out, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. That will make for an unprecedented four encounters between the Chinese and U.S. presidents in a single year. Each is another occasion for Beijing to test Trump’s resolve, now from the easier starting point of pressing him merely to hold a line he has already let slip, while angling for more.
Such waffling has real costs for the United States and Taiwan. For the U.S., the price is to the country’s reputation. A security commitment held by every administration for nearly 50 years, now treated as a “negotiating chip,” is proof to the world that no U.S. promise is safe from the next bargain. In Japan, and even more in South Korea, security rests on precisely the kind of promise Washington has just shown it will treat as negotiable. Once other governments conclude that U.S. assurances are only as good as the next election cycle, they hedge, and hedging is how the existing U.S.-led international order has already begun to come apart at the seams. 
In Taiwan itself, a large majority of Taiwanese – 85 percent in one recent poll – favor the status quo, which in practice means the island’s de facto independence. What they ask of Washington is not a harder line toward Beijing but the assurance that the United States will keep the commitments it has already made. Now simply standing by those commitments is cast as a provocation to China, rather than a continuation of existing policy. This cuts away at Taiwan’s security – a heavy cost to bear indeed.
The needed corrective is not to provoke Beijing or manufacture a confrontation over Taiwan. It is the opposite. The president himself, not an aide and not the secretary of state, should state plainly that Washington’s Taiwan policy has not changed. And he should sign the arms package, because it was never Beijing’s to veto. The Taiwan Relations Act directs that such sales be decided “based solely upon” Taiwan’s needs; on a fair reading of that language, consulting Beijing about them is difficult to square with the law in the first place. This is not about goading China. It is about standing on American law, American interest, and the near-universal wish of the people on Taiwan that the status quo endure. 
Taiwan was not bargained away at the Trump-Xi summit. But it was left on the table, within reach, and it will stay there for as long as an American president treats Taiwan as something he might one day be willing to sell.

articles.title: After the Flood, Can China, Nepal, and India Move From Earth Observation to Regional Preparedness?
articles.full_text:
A blueprint for building resilience in the Hindu Kush Himalaya.
The recent Bhotekoshi-Trishuli flood near the China-Nepal border, described as a “mountain tsunami,” occurred at a time when glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) are already melting rapidly. Extreme events like the catastrophic flood are no longer isolated anomalies but signals of a broader regional climate crisis in the fragile mountain region. Translating Earth observation of the HKH into actionable regional preparedness is therefore an urgent requirement for climate action. 
The impact was not confined to Nepal. The “mountain tsunami” obliterated Gyirong Port, the primary border crossing for both people and trading goods moving from Nepal into China. China has reported over 40 people dead and over 50 missing.
Districts along the India-Nepal border were also put on heightened alert. Indian National Disaster Response Force teams were deployed, and people in lowland areas were requested to move to safer places. And Bihar is currently dealing with a much wider flood situation. 
And floods continue to hit the region. As of September 27, at least 56 people had died in monsoon-driven flooding in India, and 14 more perished in Nepal. Several rivers, including the Ganga, Gandak, Koshi, Budhi Gandaki, and Bagmati, are above danger levels at various locations. 
Other South Asian countries are experiencing similar extreme climate events – floods and inundation. Pakistan’s disaster agency, the National Disaster Management Authority, has recorded 199 deaths since the rainfall began on June 26 of this year. Nearly 2,000 houses have been damaged. Similarly, in July, more than 1 million people were stranded across seven districts after days of heavy rain in Bangladesh.
The events of 2026 are not an aberration. The flood-risk map in the World Risk Report 2025 places Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India among the highest flood risk countries in the world.
It is also worth remembering that these events are happening in a region where per capita greenhouse gas emissions (2.5 for India, 1 for Pakistan, and 0.8 for Bangladesh) are well below the global average of 6.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per person. This raises a wider question of climate inequality, as countries contributing relatively little to global emissions face some of the greatest climate risks.
The effect of these floods – not just those on August 26, but all of them – continues long after the water recedes. As recurring floods damage crops, homes, infrastructure, commerce, and local economies, repeated losses can make it harder for families to recover. This can make farming and other local livelihoods harder to sustain in the long run, forcing the victims to opt for migration in the face of extreme vulnerability. A study conducted by the World Bank estimated that South Asia may see about 40 million internal climate migrants by 2050.
Is it possible to mitigate the damage through information sharing? That’s been a topic of much discussion since the August floods hit Nepal.
What Earth Observations Are Showing Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya
Integrated Earth observations – including visual, thermal, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) remote sensing – alongside localized field surveys demonstrate widespread cryospheric and geomorphic transformation across the broader HKH. Satellite-based observation and in situ monitoring confirm that Himalayan glaciers are experiencing persistent mass loss averaging around half a meter of ice thickness per year, accompanied by widespread snowline depression and declining snow cover. Generally, river flows are stationary, but some experience a temporary increase of discharge due to glacial ice melt. 
According to ICIMOD’s 2026 assessment, glaciers across the HKH region are losing ice at roughly twice the rate seen before 2000. Research in the Everest region shows debris-covered glaciers can experience severe thinning, surface lowering of up to 1.56 m/yr, and flow deceleration. Further, recent research indicates that the human-populated area at the Everest Base Camp has a higher surface warming rate compared to the surrounding unpopulated part of the Khumbu glaciers, a major source of the Koshi River system. 
This extensive cryospheric decay destabilizes surrounding slopes, as thawing permafrost and paraglacial moraine degradation increase susceptibility to catastrophic rock–ice avalanches and complex hazard chains. A prime example was the August 26 flood, which began with an ice–rock slope collapse from the northern face of Mount Langtang Lirung into the Chhochen Khola and Lhende Khola. The collapse induced seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake and evolved into a destructive debris flow that rushed downstream across Nepal into China and India. 
Bridging the Observation Gap: Connecting Satellites, Sensors, and Communities
Field observations and small-scale studies remain limited in the HKH due to logistical challenges, resource constraints, and field risks. Consequently, monitoring relies heavily on Earth observation and remote sensing, while long-term ground measurements of glacier mass balance, snow, and other cryospheric variables remain sparse. Cloud cover, steep terrain, and limited ground validation further constrain even satellite observations.
One study showed that glacial lakes increased in Nepal (in terms of both numbers and surface area) between 1977 and 2017. However, satellite-based inventories mainly capture such lakes’ extent and change. Gauging lake depth, volume, dam condition, and hydrological behavior often requires field measurements or higher-resolution observations.
Major gaps remain in monitoring remote glaciers, snowfields, glacial lakes, unstable terrain, and headwater rivers. The lack of data limits hazard forecasting, water resource assessments, and long-term mountain planning.
Addressing these gaps will require bringing different forms of observation together. Integrating multi-tiered Earth observations would create a comprehensive framework for monitoring dynamic cryospheric hazards across Nepal and the HKH. 
Even though satellite, SAR, and DEM data cover areas well for tracking glacier loss, tools like UAVs, CORS, and automated weather stations give much better detail at specific sites. These tools help to monitor slope instability, ice movement and hydrometeorological conditions.
Complementing these technical solutions, local community observations contribute crucial real-time contextual validation during sudden disaster events. To bridge these diverse inputs, recent scientific assessments emphasize that unifying these streams requires common geodetic reference frames, standardized data protocols, and centralized open-access platforms – such as  Mountain GeoPortal – enabling agencies like Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) to model cascading hazard chains, issue early warnings, and protect downstream river systems.
Downstream authorities and communities across Nepal and the HKH require actionable, localized, and time-sensitive warnings rather than raw scientific data or static maps. 
High-priority actionable information includes automated classifications of hazardous glacial lakes, real-time forecasts of peak flood magnitude, expected water and debris arrival times, and dynamic inundation maps highlighting at-risk settlements, roads, and hydropower facilities. 
In transboundary river basins like the Koshi and Gandak, saving lives depends on real-time cross-border hydrometeorological data sharing before flood surges cross international borders. Upstream flow warnings allow downstream operators; such as those at the Gandak Barrage-to manage control gates proactively and cushion flood impacts on plains communities. 
Ultimately, this data must feed directly into automated multi-language cell alerts and pre-rehearsed local response plans, so communities have enough time to evacuate when necessary.
From Observations to Regional Preparedness
There are already some efforts to build on. Nepal itself is now strengthening monitoring following the recent disaster, and looking for more real-time information from China on glacier movement and upstream water levels. Some of these systems may provide only a few minutes of warning during a very fast event, but even that can matter if information can reach people quickly.
There are also several existing arrangements between countries across the region for sharing flood forecasts, river data and information on mountain hazards. Some of these have been in place for decades.
Afghanistan and Pakistan cooperate through the Flash Flood Guidance System , including flood forecasting tools and technical training supported by the World Meteorological Organization.
Bangladesh and India share real-time flood data through bilateral arrangements and the Joint Rivers Commission to support flood forecasting and early warnings in Bangladesh.
articles.summary: A blueprint for building resilience in the Hindu Kush Himalaya.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Escalating Response to Cross-Border Terrorism
articles.full_text:
The recurring clashes represent the failure of months of diplomacy and external mediation. Where does the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship go from here?
Tensions are on the rise between Pakistan and Afghanistan once again as both countries have traded fire as well as accusations over the past few days. The current flare-up is a direct consequence of a terrorist attack on a mosque in the north-western Pakistani town of Kohat on September 18, in which at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, were killed and over 100 injured. 
After neutralizing the attackers after an hours-long gun battle, Pakistan launched retaliatory airstrikes against the alleged positions of the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehad ul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), which had claimed responsibility for the attack, and its ideological ally, the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in Paktika and Kunar provinces of Afghanistan on September 21. Pakistan claimed to have killed 28 terrorists in those strikes. 
Instead of engaging Pakistan’s border posts with machine guns and mortars like in most previous instances, the Taliban government of Afghanistan launched drones against Pakistan from its territory in the early hours of September 23. Eight of the drones were downed by Pakistan’s air defenses, according to Pakistani authorities. 
The Afghan drone incursions did not cause any casualties or damage to civilian or military infrastructure in Pakistan; the spokesperson for the Pakistani president dismissed them as unfrightening “flying toys.” Even so, Islamabad conducted fresh air raids in Afghanistan, targeting 10 different locations in the early hours of September 24. Pakistan’s information minister confirmed that the second round of strikes was indeed a response to the Afghan drone incursions.
Quite ironically, the Kohat terrorist attack came a day after Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, arrived in Islamabad following his trip to Afghanistan. Kalin was continuing Turkiye’s effort to mediate a long-term peace between the two countries. Kabul had already expressed its lack of enthusiasm toward the Turkish mediation when the Taliban’s Supreme Leader Mullah Hibatullah Akhunzada refused to see Kalin in Kandahar, reportedly calling him “Westernized.” Then Islamabad’s identification of one of the suicide bombers as an Afghan national and the subsequent events sealed the fate of the ongoing peace efforts by Turkiye and Qatar.
While Pakistani and Afghan security forces continue to trade fire across the border and accusations in the media, the question on many a mind right now is whether any meaningful mediation between the two countries is possible any time soon. The short answer seems to be “no.” Here is the longer explanation for it.
Looking at Pakistan’s kinetic responses to terrorist attacks that its officials associated with terrorist safe havens across the border in Afghanistan, one can discern a break from the past since October last year. Even though Islamabad has been alleging an Afghan connection to earlier terrorist attacks as well, its kinetic responses were sparse and cautious. 
Pakistan’s first reported use of force inside Afghanistan since the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021 occurred in April 2022, following a terrorist attack in the North Waziristan district bordering Afghanistan. At the time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office did not even acknowledge the airstrikes, even though the Taliban government of Afghanistan complained to the United Nations Security Council about them and initiated limited cross-border retaliatory fire against Pakistani border posts. 
Two years later, in March 2024, Pakistan once again responded with airstrikes inside Afghanistan after a terrorist attack in North Waziristan. This time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office was quick to acknowledge the attack but its spokesperson hastened to add that Islamabad “respect[ed] the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Afghanistan and look[ed] forward to working together” with Afghanistan. In a subsequent press briefing, the Foreign Office even clarified that its actions were not against the government or the people of Afghanistan. 
The response of the Taliban government of Afghanistan was also measured. Even though it claimed that it had conducted cross-border strikes against Pakistani posts, which was corroborated by the local population, the damage to personnel and infrastructure was limited. Like in April 2022, the crisis de-escalated quickly.
In December 2024 Pakistan conducted another round of airstrikes inside Afghanistan in response to a terrorist attack. Even though the airstrikes came at a time when Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan Ambassador Muhammad Sadiq was on his first visit to Kabul after resuming his responsibilities in the position, the aftermath followed a somewhat similar pattern to April 2022 and March 2024.
In October 2025, however, things changed significantly. Pakistan not only conducted an airstrike in the heart of Kabul targeting the head of the TTP, but responded to Afghanistan’s cross-border retaliatory fire on Pakistani border posts with much more intensity than the previous instances. 
This led to a quick escalation of the conflict, forcing Qatar and Turkiye to make frantic efforts toward a ceasefire as well as a longer-term rapprochement. While the ceasefire held for a time, negotiations on the signing of a longer-term peace deal between Afghanistan and Pakistan remained unsuccessful, resulting in a tense diplomatic impasse that has persisted ever since. 
Things got even worse in February 2026, when Pakistan initiated a long-term military operation aimed at neutralizing terrorists inside Afghan territory through the sustained use of air power.
Thus October 2025 marked a break from the past and February 2026 made the use of coercive power a norm. The reason for the new normal was the failure of months of bilateral and trilateral diplomacy starting in March 2025, when Sadiq travelled to Kabul again for talks after the December 2024 debacle. His visit paved the way for a visit of Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to Kabul in April. Pakistan’s Foreign Office explicitly described Dar’s visit as part of its effort to develop “good, friendly, neighborly relations” with Afghanistan. 
From May through August, Islamabad considerably intensified this diplomatic track with the involvement of China. In May, Pakistan, China, and Afghanistan held a trilateral foreign minister meeting in Beijing, where the three sides agreed to strengthen communication, economic cooperation, regional connectivity, and security cooperation. China and Pakistan also supported the extension of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) to Afghanistan. 
This was the time when Pakistan and Afghanistan also agreed to upgrade diplomatic representation from chargé d’affaires to the ambassadorial level. Dar subsequently described the diplomatic interactions as laying the foundations for a “qualitative change” in Pakistan’s bilateral relations with Afghanistan. 
On July 7, 2025, the two foreign ministries institutionalized another channel through an additional-secretary-level mechanism covering trade, transit, security, connectivity, and Afghan nationals. Dar made two back-to-back visits to Kabul in July and August to sign the framework agreement for a joint feasibility study of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway and the sixth Pakistan-China-Afghanistan trilateral, respectively. Pakistan even provided Afghanistan with humanitarian assistance after the September 2025 earthquake. 
Despite all this intense positive diplomacy, however, terrorist attacks inside Pakistan with purported links to Afghanistan continued. That is what has led Islamabad to treat coercion – not diplomacy with Afghanistan – as the primary option of choice since October 2025, even if the results of that change are highly debatable. As the escalation hurts populations on both sides of the border, there seems to be a perception among Pakistani policy circles that coercion is more likely to persuade the Afghan Taliban to quit supporting the TTP and its affiliated groups than diplomacy. And even if not, perhaps, at least Pakistan would be getting even with the Taliban. 
Tensions are on the rise between Pakistan and Afghanistan once again as both countries have traded fire as well as accusations over the past few days. The current flare-up is a direct consequence of a terrorist attack on a mosque in the north-western Pakistani town of Kohat on September 18, in which at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, were killed and over 100 injured. 
After neutralizing the attackers after an hours-long gun battle, Pakistan launched retaliatory airstrikes against the alleged positions of the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehad ul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), which had claimed responsibility for the attack, and its ideological ally, the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in Paktika and Kunar provinces of Afghanistan on September 21. Pakistan claimed to have killed 28 terrorists in those strikes. 
Instead of engaging Pakistan’s border posts with machine guns and mortars like in most previous instances, the Taliban government of Afghanistan launched drones against Pakistan from its territory in the early hours of September 23. Eight of the drones were downed by Pakistan’s air defenses, according to Pakistani authorities. 
The Afghan drone incursions did not cause any casualties or damage to civilian or military infrastructure in Pakistan; the spokesperson for the Pakistani president dismissed them as unfrightening “flying toys.” Even so, Islamabad conducted fresh air raids in Afghanistan, targeting 10 different locations in the early hours of September 24. Pakistan’s information minister confirmed that the second round of strikes was indeed a response to the Afghan drone incursions.
Quite ironically, the Kohat terrorist attack came a day after Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, arrived in Islamabad following his trip to Afghanistan. Kalin was continuing Turkiye’s effort to mediate a long-term peace between the two countries. Kabul had already expressed its lack of enthusiasm toward the Turkish mediation when the Taliban’s Supreme Leader Mullah Hibatullah Akhunzada refused to see Kalin in Kandahar, reportedly calling him “Westernized.” Then Islamabad’s identification of one of the suicide bombers as an Afghan national and the subsequent events sealed the fate of the ongoing peace efforts by Turkiye and Qatar.
While Pakistani and Afghan security forces continue to trade fire across the border and accusations in the media, the question on many a mind right now is whether any meaningful mediation between the two countries is possible any time soon. The short answer seems to be “no.” Here is the longer explanation for it.
Looking at Pakistan’s kinetic responses to terrorist attacks that its officials associated with terrorist safe havens across the border in Afghanistan, one can discern a break from the past since October last year. Even though Islamabad has been alleging an Afghan connection to earlier terrorist attacks as well, its kinetic responses were sparse and cautious. 
Pakistan’s first reported use of force inside Afghanistan since the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021 occurred in April 2022, following a terrorist attack in the North Waziristan district bordering Afghanistan. At the time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office did not even acknowledge the airstrikes, even though the Taliban government of Afghanistan complained to the United Nations Security Council about them and initiated limited cross-border retaliatory fire against Pakistani border posts. 
Two years later, in March 2024, Pakistan once again responded with airstrikes inside Afghanistan after a terrorist attack in North Waziristan. This time, Pakistan’s Foreign Office was quick to acknowledge the attack but its spokesperson hastened to add that Islamabad “respect[ed] the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Afghanistan and look[ed] forward to working together” with Afghanistan. In a subsequent press briefing, the Foreign Office even clarified that its actions were not against the government or the people of Afghanistan. 
The response of the Taliban government of Afghanistan was also measured. Even though it claimed that it had conducted cross-border strikes against Pakistani posts, which was corroborated by the local population, the damage to personnel and infrastructure was limited. Like in April 2022, the crisis de-escalated quickly.
articles.summary: The recurring clashes represent the failure of months of diplomacy and external mediation. Where does the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship go from here?

articles.title: Kyrgyz Presidential Election Set for January 2027, Candidates Start to Step Forward
articles.full_text:
So far, incumbent President Sadyr Japarov and Omurbek Suvanaliev – a politician and former minister of internal affairs – have announced their intentions to run.
Last week, Kyrgyzstan’s parliament, the Zhogorku Kenesh, officially set a date for the next presidential election: January 27, 2027. The country’s Central Election Commission (CEC) then opened the door for formal nominations.
So far, incumbent President Sadyr Japarov and Omurbek Suvanaliev – a politician and former minister of internal affairs – have announced their intentions to run. 
In August, Japarov announced that he would seek a second term, something his political surrogates have been floating for some time. Japarov was elected, formally, in January 2021 after rising from literal prison to power amid the October 2020 unrest. At the time, Kyrgyzstan’s constitution mandated a single six-year presidential term. A referendum that took place at the same time as the presidential election in 2021 ushered in what critics called the “Khanstitution,” which provides for two five-year terms for the presidency. 
In February 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s Constitutional Court clarified that Japarov’s current term does count as his first.
Japarov confirmed his ambition to seek a second term in an interview in which he also revealed that he’d initially planned for his former ally and former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, to ascend to the presidency. Japarov claimed he’d told Tashiev, “Be prepared, cleanse your circle, educate your people… Then I see: he’s not ready.”
Tashiev was convicted of a coup attempt in July, but spared a prison sentence. Prosecutors sought a harsher punishment on appeal only to have the charges reclassified and the sentence lessened further in September. He long denied any ambition to run for president. A month before his abrupt February dismissal, Tashiev responded to mounting rumors that he would seek the presidency by saying, “Many have tried and continue to try to sow discord between us, claiming that I aspire to the presidency. But this is not true… I do not intend to overthrow Sadyr Nurgoyevich [Japarov]… In this life, only death can separate us.”
Under the Kyrgyz Constitution, any citizen who is at least 35 years old, speaks the state language (Kyrgyz), and has lived in the country for at least 15 years is eligible to run for president. Potential candidates must gather at least 30,000 signatures and pay a nonrefundable fee of 1 million som (around $11,400). Individuals can nominate themselves or be nominated by a party. Under 2025 legislation, individuals with criminal records are barred from running for president. 
Suvanaliev announced his presidential ambition in a September 24 interview with RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk. Suvanaliev served as minister of internal affairs from 2006-2007 under the Kurmanbek Bakiyev administration, then as governor of Naryn from 2008-2009, among other positions over the years, many of which appear to have been related to security and law enforcement. More recently, in 2019 then-President Sooronbay Jeenbekov appointed Suvanaliev a deputy secretary in the Security Council, a position he was dismissed from in October 2020 as the Jeenbekov administration collapsed in the face of protests. Until May 2021, he was serving as a representative of the government in Batken region. 
In 2011, Suvanaliev contested for the presidency as an independent candidate. He recorded just over 16,000 votes, or 0.89 percent, in an election that Almazbek Atambayev won with 63.83 percent. 
According to Azattyk, Suvanaliev positioned himself as opposition. He said he believes that a candidate who can challenge the incumbent president should run in the elections.
Japarov said in his August interview that the door was open for anyone to run against him: “Anyone who wants to run for office can do so. As they say, go ahead. We won’t restrict anyone. The elections will be transparent, and there will be no obstacles for competitors.” 
In the country’s most recent election, a snap parliamentary poll held in November 2025, Japarov’s allies did particularly well amid a political atmosphere that observers referred to as “stifled” or dead.
As the presidential election approaches – and candidates step forward – the proof will be on the ballot and in the aftermath.

articles.title: What Did Chinese Analysts Think of the Trump-Xi Summit?
articles.full_text:
To some, Trump’s hospitality was “historic.” To others, it was an attempt to “lull China into a false sense of security.”
The flags of China and the United States during a formal welcome ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., Sep. 24, 2026.
Both in China’s official media and in the world press, the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump last week – their second so far this year – generated usual, predictable descriptions: “ambiguous,” “highly symbolic,” “historic summit,” and so on. However, a section of China’s strategic affairs community – definitely not the pro-U.S. faction – has taken exception to Trump’s “dramatic,” “personal diplomacy” hospitality in welcoming Xi. Cautioning Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leadership to tread carefully with the untrustworthy, capricious, and unpredictable Trump, a skeptic in China’s “leftist” media even observed, “It’s possible they’re [the U.S.] trying to lull China into a false sense of security.”
U.S. watchers in mainland China are split into two factions: pro-U.S. (qin-Mei) and anti-U.S. (fan-Mei). The qin-Mei faction among the Chinese intelligentsia, as expected, celebrated Trump personally greeting the Chinese leader at the airport, as well as the grand welcoming ceremony and the meticulously arranged state banquet at the White House. 
“The U.S. side welcomed the Chinese leader with a level of courtesy rarely seen in recent years,” a qin-Mei-leaning Chinese language media outlet reported as Xi returned home. 
Some scholars in China highlighted the “historic” and “diplomatic” significance that Trump served Xi the same wine that former U.S. President Richard Nixon used during his visit to China in 1972. In an interview with a popular digital e-paper published from Shanghai, Professor Wu Xinbo, the director of the Center for American Studies at the city’s Fudan University, noted, “The serving of the same wine Nixon used during his China visit in the early 1970s indicates that the current China-U.S. relationship is at an important and historically significant juncture, and President Xi’s visit is historic and a milestone.” 
Further, it was widely reported in China that following a tea reception held at the White House for Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, Trump remarked: “The United States was very pleased with this visit, and that the visit has been very productive.” Asked why Trump placed such importance on Xi’s visit, Wu said: “Interactions outside of formal talks, whether it’s taking a walk, having tea, or visiting culturally and historically significant sites, can create a relaxed and informal atmosphere for the leaders of both countries.” 
Notably, Wu was invited to attend the state banquet welcoming Trump in Beijing earlier in May this year. Hence, it is understandable that he attaches great importance to opportunities leaders create beyond formal meetings.
At another level, some scholars in China, especially economists, see the current friction in China-U.S. relations arising out of “imbalance” in the economies of the world’s two largest powers. Addressing the issue of the need for “balance” and “equilibrium” between China and the United States at a recent economists’ forum on the eve of Xi’s Washington visit, Professor Ju Jiandong of Tsinghua University in Beijing said: “The currently existing extreme pattern of China doing manufacturing and the United States doing finance is inherently unstable, which is the root cause of the competition between China and the United States.” The Tsinghua professor recently published a controversial book, “The Great Power Competition and the Restructuring of World Order,” in which he argued that the “only way for China and the U.S. to avoid a lose-lose situation is to move from hegemonic iterations to competitive coexistence.”
In sharp contrast, scholars belonging to the fan-Mei faction in China have become more suspicious of the United States given Trump’s “rare, dramatic” personal touch in welcoming the Chinese leader. Scholars in this camp pointed out two examples of Trump going out of his way to impress. One, Trump made a great show of personally greeting Xi at the airport, at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington, D.C. The last time a U.S. president personally welcomed a foreign leader in this manner was 11 years ago, when Barack Obama met Pope Francis at the airport in 2015. Earlier, in 1962, John F. Kennedy had similarly welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.
The other dramatic event that particularly drew attention from the Chinese skeptics was Trump making some startling remarks at the banquet welcoming the Chinese head of state. Citing reports widely circulated in Chinese media, one commentary noted Trump “shamelessly” declaring that the relationship between the two countries has never been as harmonious as it is now. Reacting adversely to the word “harmonious,” the commentary called it “a remarkable attempt by U.S. President Trump to whitewash the current state of the relationship.”  
Three factors explain this skepticism targeting Trump and his theatrics while hosting Xi. First, as mentioned, China’s skeptics are apprehensive of China being lulled into a false sense of security. Characterizing Trump as a leader who is “two-faced and hypocritical,” these scholars assert that Trump cannot be trusted. They want CCP leaders to always be vigilant of “untrustworthy” Trump. As the commentary cited above put it: “Trump acted this way towards Russia, and he did the same toward Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela. Regarding China, he has repeatedly attacked over the years, displaying the same ugly nature of a two-faced and hypocritical person.”
Second, some in China suspect Trump’s lavish reception of Xi was a tactic to sow discord between China and Russia. It is argued that Trump has always been outspoken about breaking up the close relationship between China and Russia, seeking to isolate them. These Chinese scholars further argue that before his “dramatic” hospitality toward Xi, Trump was on record in making efforts to cultivate the most “harmonious” Russia-U.S. relationship possible. However, that attempt backfired, resulting in domestic criticism and accusations of collusion with Russia. Now, he’s elevating the China-U.S. relationship to an unprecedented level. 
Some in China are even drawing parallels between Trump’s statement praising unprecedented harmony in China-U.S. relations at present with the historic scenario of the United States and China joining forces against the Soviet Union. 
“This baseless accusation is not without purpose; its direct effect is to place China-U.S. relations above China-Russia relations, while still maintaining a strong intention to dismantle them,” scholar Zhang Zhikun argued.
Third, some Chinese skeptics are putting forward what appears to be bizarre logic: Trump’s attempt to “whitewash” China-U.S. relations are aimed to stabilize ties so that the United States can act without restraint. Scholars advancing this argument acknowledge that a section of the media and political elite in the United States is highly critical of Trump’s “subservient” approach toward Xi. However, given Trump’s capricious and ambitious nature, it is extremely difficult to fathom the U.S. leader’s true intentions. The fan-Mei faction vehemently argues that “he [Trump] is using appeasement to stabilize [relations with] China, allowing the U.S. to act with greater impunity and wage war around the world.”
To sum up, it is quite clear Trump has succeeded in further deepening the divide between rival qin-Mei and fan-Mei factions among Chinese foreign policy experts, especially the U.S. watchers in China. They interpret the summit – and its implications for China – quite differently.
The two Chinese factions do have one thing in common: they share the viewpoint that changes in Sino-U.S. relations will inevitably lead to corresponding changes in relations among countries around the world. Many Chinese scholars agree that any change in the highly complex China-U.S. relations will not affect Taiwan and Japan, as the two have “secured” their respective interests vis-a-vis the United States. However, some Chinese scholars are of the opinion that changes in China-U.S. relations will lead North Korea to gravitate toward Russia and India toward the United States.

articles.title: Rahul Bajoria, BofA India Chief Economist, on India’s Manufacturing Ambitions
articles.full_text:
Why has India’s manufacturing sector has remained stuck at around 15 percent of GDP despite decades of rapid growth?
Rahul Bajoria, head of India and ASEAN Economic Research at Bank of America, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine why India’s manufacturing sector has remained stuck at around 15 percent of GDP despite decades of rapid growth. 
They discuss the colonial and planning-era roots of India’s weak industrial base, the regulatory and compliance burdens that keep Indian firms small and push them into informality, why regulatory progress has been driven by a handful of competitive states rather than by the center, India’s limited gains from China Plus One and its growing exports to China, the mixed record of production-linked incentives and the scaling up of the Apple ecosystem, and the electricity, labor and land reforms needed to lift manufacturing to 25 percent of GDP by 2047.
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.
