articles.title: Why Has the Maldives Inserted Itself Into the Chagos Sovereignty Dispute?
articles.full_text:
Muizzu has promised to submit evidence supporting the Maldives’ claim to Chagos to relevant international bodies.
Maldivian President Dr Mohamed Muizzu addresses a Cabinet meeting at Male, Maldives, June 23, 2024.
It is official government policy under President Mohamed Muizzu that the Maldives has the strongest claim to the Chagos Islands. His is the first Maldivian administration to assert sovereignty over the archipelago, located in the central Indian Ocean and home to the joint U.K.-U.S. military base on Diego Garcia.
In doing so, Muizzu has inserted the Maldives into the long-running dispute between the United Kingdom and Mauritius over sovereignty over Chagos.
Chagos was administered as a dependency of British Mauritius from 1814 until 1965. That year, three years before Mauritius gained independence, Britain separated the archipelago from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) and establish the military base on Diego Garcia. The Chagossian population was then brutally expelled to make way for the base.
The separation ran counter to decolonization principles barring the dismemberment of colonial territories before independence.
Mauritius has objected ever since and, in recent years, has seen international law and global public opinion turn in its favor. In 2019, the International Court of Justice concluded that Mauritius’ decolonization had not been lawfully completed and that Britain should end its administration “as rapidly as possible.” That same year, the United Nations General Assembly overwhelmingly endorsed that position by 116 votes to six.
Mounting pressure eventually led Britain to negotiate with Mauritius, culminating in a 2025 treaty that recognized Mauritian sovereignty while retaining Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease arrangement. Yet the deal remains stalled amid British political opposition and U.S. concerns over the base’s security and continued operation.
Amid these negotiations, the Muizzu administration has asserted that neither the U.K. nor Mauritius has the strongest claim to Chagos, the Maldives does. It therefore opposes any transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius while its own claim remains unresolved.
Muizzu raised this objection in letters to the U.K. government in November 2024 and January 2026, with then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy in December 2025, and again in a September 2026 letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham seeking talks.
The government’s case is nebulous. It rests principally on a 16th-century document in which the exiled Sultan Hassan IX claimed title to the “seven islands of Pullobay,” identified in the Maldives with Foalhavahi, or Chagos. The government also cites Maldivian folklore, alleged centuries-old gravestones bearing Dhivehi script, and the islands’ proximity to the Maldives.
The claim also has no precedent in Maldivian diplomacy. In more than 60 years since independence, no previous administration has claimed sovereignty over Chagos.
Previously, Maldivian concerns centered on maritime boundaries, as the Maldives’ EEZ overlapped with waters claimed on the basis of Chagos. Malé kept its position on Chagos sovereignty ambiguous, dealing with either the U.K. or Mauritius depending on which better served its interests. It entered delimitation talks with the U.K. in 1992 and joined Mauritius in a 2011 communiqué opposing the U.K.’s marine protected area around Chagos, which restricted fishing.
The claim of sovereignty over Chagos itself has its origins in the politics surrounding the 2023 presidential election. Opponents of then President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih began conflating the Maldives’ EEZ dispute with Mauritius with the separate issue of sovereignty over Chagos.
The controversy began after it emerged that Solih had written to Mauritian Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth in August 2022, recognizing Mauritius’ sovereignty over Chagos. This reversed the Maldives’ earlier position as one of only six countries to oppose the 2019 United Nations General Assembly resolution endorsing the ICJ opinion in favor of Mauritius’ claim to Chagos.
Solih’s shift appears to have reflected the growing international legal recognition of Mauritius’ claim. During maritime delimitation proceedings initiated by Mauritius before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the Maldives argued that the case could not proceed while sovereignty over Chagos remained disputed between Mauritius and the U.K.
ITLOS dismissed that objection, treating sovereignty over Chagos as settled in favor of Mauritius.
Once Solih’s letter became public, however, the dispute turned sharply political.
His opponents argued that recognizing Mauritius’ claim weakened the Maldives’ case before ITLOS. Although the tribunal’s final ruling in April 2023 awarded the Maldives slightly more of the disputed maritime area than Mauritius, the opposition portrayed the outcome as a loss of Maldivian territory.
The rhetoric escalated when the EEZ dispute became entangled with a new sovereignty claim. Former President Mohamed Nasheed, then locked in an internal struggle with President Solih within the ruling MDP, argued that the Maldives itself had a claim to Chagos and that Solih had betrayed Maldivian interests by recognizing Mauritius’ claim. Former President Abdulla Yameen and the opposition Progressive Party of Maldives (PPM) soon adopted the same position. Neither, however, had advanced such a claim while in office.
It was in this political context that Muizzu inherited the issue and turned it into government policy. After Yameen was barred from contesting the 2023 election, Muizzu led the PPM-People’s National Congress (PNC) coalition to victory on a nationalist platform built around defending Maldivian sovereignty.
Alongside the “India Out” campaign, he pledged to recover the Maldives’ “lost” maritime territory. In office, that rhetoric hardened into policy. Muizzu rejected the final ITLOS judgment on the maritime boundary and became the first incumbent Maldivian administration to assert sovereignty over Chagos itself.
Muizzu has formally withdrawn Solih’s 2022 letter supporting Mauritius’ claim and promised to submit evidence supporting the Maldives’ claim to Chagos to relevant international bodies. He has also created a new government office to oversee territorial boundaries and related disputes.
Perhaps most dramatically, in February the government deployed Coast Guard vessels and drones across the full 200-nautical-mile zone it claims, including waters awarded to Mauritius by ITLOS, and intercepted Sri Lankan fishing vessels there. Despite the theatrics, the ITLOS judgment on the maritime boundary is final and not subject to ordinary appeal. Repeating such deployments in waters assigned to Mauritius would therefore risk turning a settled legal dispute into an international incident.
Nor do these actions advance the Maldives’ separate sovereignty claim over Chagos, which has so far gained no international traction. The U.K. has shown little inclination to entertain it, reiterating that Chagos sovereignty remains a bilateral matter between the U.K. and Mauritius and does not concern the Maldives.
Mauritius, meanwhile, suspended diplomatic relations with the Maldives in February 2026.
For now, then, the claim’s clearest impact is domestic rather than international. It allows Muizzu to place Chagos within a broader political narrative about defending Maldivian sovereignty and recovering territory supposedly lost by previous governments. Internationally, however, the claim has yet to alter either the legal or diplomatic landscape surrounding Chagos.
It is official government policy under President Mohamed Muizzu that the Maldives has the strongest claim to the Chagos Islands. His is the first Maldivian administration to assert sovereignty over the archipelago, located in the central Indian Ocean and home to the joint U.K.-U.S. military base on Diego Garcia.
In doing so, Muizzu has inserted the Maldives into the long-running dispute between the United Kingdom and Mauritius over sovereignty over Chagos.
Chagos was administered as a dependency of British Mauritius from 1814 until 1965. That year, three years before Mauritius gained independence, Britain separated the archipelago from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) and establish the military base on Diego Garcia. The Chagossian population was then brutally expelled to make way for the base.
articles.summary: Muizzu has promised to submit evidence supporting the Maldives’ claim to Chagos to relevant international bodies.

articles.title: US Republicans Weren’t Happy With Trump’s Hosting of Xi
articles.full_text:
A spate of Republican senators took umbrage at Trump’s reception of “a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.”
U.S. Senator Thom Tillis during a congressional delegation visit to Taipei, Taiwan, Mar. 29, 2026.
Surrounding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, D.C. – capped by a summit at the White House with U.S. President Donald Trump – was a spate of commentary from both sides of the political aisle. Clearly, not everyone was convinced of the need for Xi to visit in the first place.
Even Trump loyalists such as Louisiana Senator John Kennedy spoke out against having Xi at the White House.  One of the Senate’s most colorfully spoken members, Kennedy made his point of view known in no uncertain terms, speaking on the Will Cain show.
Kennedy opined: “All four of them are the same. It’s like the same hooker in different dresses. They all lie like time share salesmen. You can’t trust ‘em.  You can’t turn your back on any of ‘em, even if I thought, I knew they were two days dead.”
Kennedy was referring to the leaders of China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia – Xi Jinping, Masoud Pezeshkian, Kim Jong Un, and Vladimir Putin, respectively.
Kennedy went on to dub the quartet “a colony of reptiles,” giving Xi pride of place as the “chief reptile” and “quarterback.”
Taking a more serious approach from his powerful perch as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Mississippi Senator Roger Wicker, also a strong Trump supporter, forcefully stated his opposition to the state visit and summit. From the Senate floor, Wicker said, “Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.” 
The Senate Armed Services Committee carries enormous influence and prestige in Washington and beyond, and Wicker used that platform to call out Trump’s decision to bring Xi to Washington, and roll out the red carpet for him.
Key among the core functions of the committee itself is responsibility for aeronautical and space activities associated with the development of weapons systems, and for the Departments of Defense, Army, Navy, and Air Force. It also oversees military research and development.  
With that authority behind him, Wicker said, “I want to take a moment to suggest a list of topics that the president might mention during the summit.”
“This summer,” he continued, “it was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence, and that intelligence led to the death of American troops. So I would certainly suggest that the president try to get an answer to that.”
Wicker’s list continued. He wanted answers on the plight of the Uyghur people, along with Tibetan Buddhists, Christians, and Falun Gong practitioners. “Why not suggest,” Wicker reflected, “releasing all imprisoned Christians and allowing all people of whatever faith to worship freely?”
Finally, Wicker listed the abuses by China of its neighbors, of Taiwan, of Hong Kong, of African nations, of dissidents, and of Jimmy Lai, the 78-year old former Hong Kong newspaper publisher who ran afoul of security laws pushed through by Beijing and who is now serving a 20-year sentence for sedition and collusion with foreign forces.  
Wicker continued, “During every minute of dialogue, our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Joining the chorus, North Carolina Republican Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on September 24 – the day of the summit and state dinner – that Trump’s hosting of Xi was “bad timing.”
Calling the meeting a “WTF moment,” Tillis questioned why Xi had received a red-carpet welcome that surpassed those given to traditional U.S. allies.
Axios reported that Tillis was “worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations.”
“It’s not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation,” Tillis said. “Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview.”
Tillis went on to question what prompted the “sea change” he sees in Trump’s posture toward China after years of pledging to take a hard line against Beijing.
The White House downplayed the criticism from the Republican senators, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly pointing out that Trump was “reciprocating” the “hospitality” Xi showed when Trump visited China in May.
It could be argued that it is less hypocritical to honor Xi with a state dinner than not. The reasons are myriad. From 1990 through 2020, the United States invested $284 billion into Xi’s country, not including venture capital. And, according to the Global Times, there are over 84,000 U.S.-invested companies in China.  
Notably, the United States has educated over 3 million Chinese students since visas became available in the late 1970s.   
And, as strong as the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is, its belief and behavioral systems have had to radically alter in order to build an economy that serves the people well enough to keep the CCP in power.
The CCP has had to abandon the command economy that is central to communist countries in favor of a fusion economy that blends state-owned enterprises, private domestically owned enterprises, and importantly, foreign-owned enterprises. It is the latter, the foreign-owned enterprises, that have brought about profound changes to the mindset and living standards of much of the Chinese population. By manufacturing in China products never seen before in the country, whether for domestic use or export, or both, China experienced a rapid modernization by exposure to the products themselves, the processes and standards of quality required to manufacture them, and the labor standards and management styles that make those businesses profitable.
Perhaps, then, instead of focusing on a state dinner for a Chinese leader little trusted in the United States, it is more fitting to view that dinner and the pomp and ceremony that surrounded it as a state dinner in honor of the Chinese people. They have had to put up with a lot, and still do. They may not have had a seat at the table in the White House, but they will have viewed with pride the American treatment of a Chinese leader. Diplomatically, and historically, that goes a long way.

Even Trump loyalists such as Louisiana Senator John Kennedy spoke out against having Xi at the White House.  One of the Senate’s most colorfully spoken members, Kennedy made his point of view known in no uncertain terms, speaking on the Will Cain show.
Kennedy opined: “All four of them are the same. It’s like the same hooker in different dresses. They all lie like time share salesmen. You can’t trust ‘em.  You can’t turn your back on any of ‘em, even if I thought, I knew they were two days dead.”

articles.title: Pakistan and Terrorism: When the Tables Turn
articles.full_text:
Islamabad cannot use its own people’s suffering to erase its record of supporting forces that have devastated lives in other countries.
In his address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described Afghanistan as a haven for terrorist groups carrying out attacks against Pakistan. He specifically named Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or the TTP, and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and called on the Afghan Taliban to take decisive action to prevent Afghan soil from being used against Pakistan and other countries. 
Coming from a Pakistani official, this demand raises many questions. The first is: since when has Pakistan decided that supporting armed groups in a neighboring country is dangerous? When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan against the Republic government and the Afghan people were the victims, where was this concern? Why does the same government that supported the Taliban for years now speak about terrorist sanctuaries as though it had no role in creating this situation?
Pakistan’s support for the Taliban is not merely an allegation made by Afghans out of anger or without grounding. Financial support, the training and recruitment of fighters, the transfer of ammunition and fuel, and cooperation between Pakistani military and intelligence officials and the Taliban have been extensively documented over the years by credible international organizations. For much of the last 25 years, Pakistan helped strengthen a force that imposed war and repression on the people of Afghanistan.
The Haqqani network is a clear example of this conduct. Its sanctuaries in North Waziristan and its ties to Pakistan’s intelligence apparatus have been the subject of reports and official objections for years. In 2011, Mike Mullen, then chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, described the network as effectively an arm of Pakistani intelligence, an allegation Islamabad denied. Now that Pakistan is complaining about sanctuaries across the border, it must explain why it refused to meet the same demand regarding the Haqqani network more than a decade ago.
Even after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, then-Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan spoke of Afghans breaking the “shackles of slavery.” The political meaning of this response was clear: the Taliban’s victory was welcomed in Islamabad. But now that the Taliban are not behaving as Pakistan expected, that same victory has become a threat. Has the Taliban’s nature only just become apparent, or has Pakistan’s calculation that it could control the Taliban’s behavior simply proved wrong?
To me, this reversal shows that the central problem is a selective definition of terrorism. When the Taliban were fighting in Afghanistan and helping expand Pakistan’s influence, justifications could be found for supporting them. Now that groups close to the Taliban are fighting against Pakistan, Islamabad is suddenly concerned about sanctuaries, support, and the responsibility of the host state. Human lives should not suddenly become valuable simply because the place where people are killed has changed.
Of course, the people of Pakistan are, indeed, the victims of terrorism. No disagreement with Islamabad’s policies can justify killing Pakistani citizens. The TTP is a real threat and must be confronted. But the same standard must also apply to victims in Afghanistan and India of groups supported by Pakistan. Pakistan’s government cannot use its own people’s suffering to erase its record of supporting forces that have devastated lives in other countries.
Pakistan’s hostility toward the TTP is not new. It has conducted operations against the TTP and other groups that target Pakistan. The issue, therefore, is not that Islamabad has never fought terrorism; it is why its response to armed groups has varied depending on where their attacks are directed. If opposition to terrorism is a matter of principle, networks that recruit fighters, raise funds and organize attacks against neighboring countries must be viewed as equally unacceptable.
As long as this contradiction remains, Pakistan’s statements about terrorism cannot be taken seriously. That can only change if Pakistan moves beyond general statements and actually fights terrorism, something it appears to have no intention of doing. Lashkar-e-Taiba is one of the clearest examples. The U.N. Security Council’s sanctions committee identifies this Pakistan-based group as responsible for numerous attacks against military and civilian targets, including the 2008 Mumbai attacks. The same records identify Jamaat-ud-Dawa, also based in Pakistan, as a front for financing, training and supporting Lashkar-e-Taiba.
Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) is another example. Founded by Masood Azhar after his release from prison in India, the group is on the U.N. sanctions list, too. The Security Council has documented its links with al-Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its role in attacks in Kashmir. In May 2025, JeM was reported to be based in Bahawalpur, in Pakistan’s Punjab province.
Hizbul Mujahideen is another longstanding group active in Kashmir, fighting to end Indian rule and unite the region with Pakistan. According to U.S. State Department reports, the group has carried out numerous attacks against Indian security personnel and politicians and has been involved in abductions and killings. Reports from June 2026 also describe its leader, Syed Salahuddin, as being based in Pakistan.
Harakat-ul-Mujahideen is another example of these cross-border networks. The Security Council’s records identify Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi as bases for the group and record attacks against military and civilian targets in Kashmir, the training of fighters and cooperation with other groups. The hijacking of an Indian aircraft in 1999 has also been attributed to the group. This history shows that the connection between Pakistan-based groups and violence across the region has not been limited to the Afghan Taliban and stretched across decades.
In April 2025, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif was asked in an interview with Sky News about the country’s history of supporting, training and financing terrorist groups. He replied: “We have been doing this dirty work for the United States for about three decades, and the West, including Britain.” He called this policy a mistake and spoke about its costs for Pakistan. But what about the price the people of Afghanistan have paid? How does pointing to the role of the United States and the U.K. remove the responsibility of Pakistani officials?
If Pakistan wants its words to be taken seriously, it must demonstrate at home the same thing it demands of the Taliban: action against international terrorism and measures that can be verified. The fight against terrorism has credibility when past political ties to a group do not stand in the way of action against it. Pakistan’s statements about terrorism can be taken seriously only when it acts to cut off funding, stop recruitment and dismantle the operational structures of known terrorist groups on its own soil.
Until then, these words will remain just words; neither the problem of terrorism in Pakistan nor the threat that has driven it to make these statements will go away. Otherwise, the very danger then U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned about in 2011 will persist: “You can’t keep snakes in your backyard and expect them only to bite your neighbors.” 
It is the continuation of this same policy that makes Pakistan’s language about terrorism difficult to take seriously in 2026.
Islamabad wants an end to the threat directed at itself, but it must show that it judges its neighbors’ security by the same standard. Terrorism was no less dangerous or criminal when it helped extend Pakistan’s influence. To give its words credibility, Pakistan must demonstrate that its concern is terrorism itself, even when terrorists are fighting against another country.
So far, what we can see is that Pakistan’s current dispute with the Taliban does not, in itself, mean it has abandoned its longstanding policy of using armed groups to further its aims. The test of change is an end to the logic of using such groups. If Islamabad raises its voice only when these groups defy its wishes, what has changed is the relationship between the patron and the group; the value of human life is still judged by the same selective standard.
Before Sharif describes Afghanistan as a haven for terrorism, he must explain what role his own country has played in bringing Afghanistan to this point. The people of Afghanistan never invited Pakistan to support the Taliban, and they should not now have to pay the price for that failed calculation.

articles.title: South Korean Submarines Could Save Australia From the AUKUS Shambles
articles.full_text:
Could the conventionally-powered KSS-III sub offer a more affordable and timely alternative to the planned nuclear-powered fleet?
South Korean submarine ROKS Park Wi arrives at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam for routine training in the Hawaiian operations area and preparations for the Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) exercise, June 1, 2018.
In July, the Canadian government announced that it has chosen the German-Norwegian bid to build 12 conventionally-powered submarines to replace their obsolete Victoria class fleet. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reported the estimated cost of the submarines at CA$24 billion. With 35-year lifetime maintenance and sustainment costs added, the overall program cost is likely to be in the vicinity of CA$100 billion. This compares more than favorably to the A$368 billion (the dollar equivalents are similar) allocated so far to AUKUS.
The Canadians said they had a hard time choosing between two excellent options – the other being the South Korean KSS-III submarine.
Professor Hugh White has long experience with our Collins class submarine project and, more recently, with the details of AUKUS. He says that as an alternative to the AUKUS project “any off-the-shelf submarines Australia could get its hands on, we should take.”
One option is to turn back to the French Naval Group for a new order of 12 submarines. In evidence given to the AUKUS public inquiry in Canberra on 2 September, retired admiral Peter Briggs gave an informed presentation on the capabilities of nuclear-powered submarines. He favors procurement of a low-enriched uranium nuclear-powered submarine, based on the French Suffren class, for the Royal Australian Navy (RAN). He strongly opposes purchase of the US Virginia class and the proposed British-designed SSN AUKUS boats, describing the plan as “flawed and undeliverable”.
His conclusion about the AUKUS submarines is widely supported by the evidence and a strong consensus of military and academic opinion.
During his presentation Admiral Briggs stated his view that conventional diesel-electric submarine technology was not acceptable for the next generation of RAN operations. His argument was that conventionally powered submarines have neither the stealth features nor the endurance needed for effective undersea naval operations. Nonetheless, the example he cited concerned the limitations of the existing Collins class submarine design. As is well known, Collins is an outdated platform that is nearing the end of its operational life.
Given the South Koreans only recently lost the bid for 12 submarines to replace the ageing Canadian fleet, their new submarine should be available for export without delay. The KSS-III proposal had an appealing range of handover deadlines promised for Canada. The expected first boat delivery date was scheduled to be 2032, with the initial batch of four submarines delivered by 2035 and the remaining eight boats at the rate of one per year until 2043, when the entire fleet of 12 would be in service. It has been reported that the South Korean tender may have suffered a disadvantage because Canadian infrastructure and crew capacity to absorb the fleet in that timeframe is underdeveloped. This is much less a problem in Australia.
These delivery timeframes compare to 2032 proposed for the first second-hand AUKUS Virginia; thereafter delivery in 2035 and 2038 respectively. The first British-designed AUKUS SSN boat is not expected to be delivered until the fuzzy “2040s.” Obviously, procurement of an entire one-class fleet of 12 KSS-III submarines by 2043 is an attractive option. It would adequately cover the capability gap of decommissioned Collins class submarines, scheduled to begin in 2040. If the argument about needing more naval capability now has any relevance, early delivery is a must.
Defence Central is the authoritative London-based bureau for published defence intelligence. They produce “deep-dive reports on procurement, weaponry and integrated command structures”.
Defence Central notes that in 2021 South Korea became the first country without nuclear weapons to successfully test a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM). The launch came from the Dosan Anh Changho, the first KSS-III class submarine produced. South Korea’s KSS-III program represents the third phase of the country’s indigenous submarine development strategy. Earlier phases relied heavily on German technology. The KSS-III represents a leap forward to a fully domestic design capable of supporting strategic missions, including nuclear deterrence.
The KSS-III supersedes two earlier models in both size and capability. Measuring 83.5 meters in length with a beam of 9.7 meters, the submarine has a submerged displacement of approximately 3,800 tons. It is powered by a diesel-electric propulsion system with an air-independent propulsion module that allows for greater submerged endurance compared to conventional diesel-electric submarines. The crew complement needed is 50 people – a massive reduction on the 135 sailors required to operate the US Virginia class boats – and the 100 crew required for the 10,000-ton SSN AUKUS boats, should they ever reach naval service.
The design configuration allows the KSS-III to remain submerged for up to 20 days without surfacing, a key feature for survivability in contested waters. The boat has a top submerged speed of 37 kph, or 20 knots, and an operational range of around 19,000 kilometers. These specifications allow for long patrols in both coastal and open sea environments. The latest version boats are also capable of generating electricity underwater to recharge their fuel cell batteries. This enables long underwater voyages and obviates the need for frequent “snorts,” when the submarine has to come to the surface and potentially reveal its position to an enemy satellite.
One of the defining features of the KSS-III is its vertical launch system (VLS). It is the first South Korean submarine equipped with a VLS capable of deploying a battery of underwater-launched missiles. The Korean-designed Hyunmoo-3 cruise missiles offer a credible second-strike capability, especially relevant given the regional missile capabilities of North Korea and China. The Hyunmoo-3 is roughly equivalent to the US Navy’s Tomahawk but is supersonic, with a reported speed of Mach 1.2. In addition to SLBMs, the KSS-III can carry heavyweight torpedoes and anti-ship missiles launched from its standard torpedo tubes.
The newest design KSS-III, known as Batch 2 submarines, will have an increased displacement of approximately 4,000 tons and an expanded VLS capable of carrying up to ten missiles. They will also feature enhanced sonar systems, improved stealth characteristics and a more advanced combat management platform. Batch 2 construction is already under way, with the second unit expected to be launched this year.
The new boats also feature advanced anechoic tiles covering their HY-100 steel hulls to suppress underwater radiated noise and reduce active/passive sonar detectability. The K-111 class submarines are part of South Korea’s three-axis defense system, a strategy aimed at detecting, intercepting and retaliating against missile threats. The inclusion of SLBM capability on a conventional submarine makes the KSS-III unique.
Should the AUKUS public inquiry find that a non-nuclear-powered alternative to the Collins class is a desirable option for Australia’s defense, it is manifest that the KSS-III should be considered as a replacement. The independent publication Naval News describes the KSS-III as “the most potent conventionally powered and armed submarine in the world”. The cost is much more affordable; its performance is outstanding; it has none of the problems associated with nuclear waste disposal and security – and it can be delivered on a much faster schedule than the AUKUS boats.
Perhaps more importantly than all of this, discontinuing the purchase of AUKUS nuclear attack submarines surely removes a powerful incentive for China to attack Australia.
This article was originally published by the website Pearls and Irritations and is reprinted with permission.

The first British-designed AUKUS SSN boat is not expected to be delivered until the fuzzy “2040s.” Obviously, procurement of an entire one-class fleet of 12 KSS-III submarines by 2043 is an attractive option. It would adequately cover the capability gap of decommissioned Collins class submarines, scheduled to begin in 2040. If the argument about needing more naval capability now has any relevance, early delivery is a must.
Defence Central is the authoritative London-based bureau for published defence intelligence. They produce “deep-dive reports on procurement, weaponry and integrated command structures”.
Defence Central notes that in 2021 South Korea became the first country without nuclear weapons to successfully test a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM). The launch came from the Dosan Anh Changho, the first KSS-III class submarine produced. South Korea’s KSS-III program represents the third phase of the country’s indigenous submarine development strategy. Earlier phases relied heavily on German technology. The KSS-III represents a leap forward to a fully domestic design capable of supporting strategic missions, including nuclear deterrence.
articles.summary: Could the conventionally-powered KSS-III sub offer a more affordable and timely alternative to the planned nuclear-powered fleet?

articles.title: Vietnam Confirms Arrest of Viet Tan Activists Reported Missing in Cambodia
articles.full_text:
Rights groups claim that Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep were abducted in Cambodia, in line with a pattern of growing transnational repression by the Vietnamese state.
Vietnam has confirmed the arrest of two foreign activists reported missing in neighboring Cambodia earlier this month, whom rights group claim were abducted by the Vietnamese authorities.
The Ministry of Public Security said yesterday that its Security Investigation Agency had detained three men after they “entered Vietnam illegally from Cambodia,” the state-run newspaper Tuoi Tre reported.
Nguyen Duc Thuan, 52, Ho Pham Hiep Huy (also known as Tran Hiep), 51, and Thai Cong Truong Son, 46, are under investigation for “Terrorism” under Article 299 of the Penal Code and “Forging seals and documents of agencies and organizations” under Article 341.
Under questioning, the three confessed to being members of Viet Tan, a U.S.-based pro-democracy group that the Ministry described as a “terrorist organization.” It said that they also admitted to “carrying fake documents to illegally enter Việt Nam to conduct terrorist and sabotage activities.”
The Ministry’s announcement came after Thuan, a Norwegian citizen, and Hiep, an Australian citizen, were reported missing in Phnom Penh by Viet Tan earlier this month. In an alert dated September 25, the organization, which says that it advocates a “peaceful, nonviolent struggle” for democracy in Vietnam, said that the two men had been missing in Cambodia since September 18.
Thuan and Hiep had arrived in Phnom Penh from Bangkok on September 15 and were due to leave Cambodia on September 19, but never boarded their flights, Viet Tan spokesperson Duy Hoang told Cambodia’s Kiripost news site. Hoang added that the pair came to Cambodia to meet with Vietnamese human rights defenders who lived in the country.
Viet Tan, which was formed by South Vietnamese exiles in 1982, is high on the hitlist of the communist authorities, who remain paranoid about any advocacy that is even tangentially linked to the cause of the defunct southern Republic of Vietnam.
After the arrest of the pair, Viet Tan accused the Vietnamese authorities of abducting Thuan and Hiep from Cambodia.
“Viet Tan strongly condemns the abduction of two of its members in Cambodia and the fabricated charges issued by the Vietnamese communist authorities to cover up an act of transnational repression,” it said in a statement yesterday. The Ministry of Public’s Security’s claim that the two men were arrested for entering Vietnam illegally was a “a blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam,” it added.

articles.title: The Global Data Center Boom Has Arrived in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
Will the region’s demand for artificial intelligence services justify the enormous outlays of money and resources?
Processing and storing data is now pushing the frontier of economic development around the world, and huge amounts of capital are flowing into building out the infrastructure to support this big bet on cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence. The race to establish an advantageous position on the digital frontier is driving a major capex boom in the United States and elsewhere, and this wave has now fully arrived in Southeast Asia.
Data centers require substantial land and resources, like electricity and water, and they need reliable connectivity such as access to subsea cable networks. Countries that have land, reasonably well-developed energy and telecommunications infrastructure and friendly regulatory environments are attracting investors and developers looking to ride the data center wave. Affordable inputs, like electricity, can sweeten the deal. It just so happens that many countries in Southeast Asia fit this bill.
Malaysia is leading the pack. Clear policy guidance, well-developed infrastructure and close proximity to land-constrained Singapore are helping fuel a boom in data centers. The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone has seen a flurry of activity, but it is part of a broader phenomenon. In the first quarter of 2023, the Department of Statistics recorded a cumulative $11 billion of foreign investment in the information and communication sector, accounting for 5 percent of total foreign investment. By first quarter of 2026, this figure had risen to $32.5 billion, equal to 12 percent of total inbound investment.
And there is no sign of slowing. According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the body that reviews and approves investment projects, between 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, $96 billion worth of data center and cloud computing projects were approved, including $24 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. These are project approvals rather than realized investment, but it gives a sense of the speed and scale at which the data center boom is unfolding across Malaysia.
Indonesia is also seeing an uptick in data center investment. Like Malaysia, some of this is driven by demand from Singapore, particularly in and around the island of Batam. Nongsa Digital Park is a Special Economic Zone that offers eligible projects tax and other fiscal incentives. Combined with Batam’s strong subsea cable connectivity, this has fueled a wave of new data center construction in the area.
There is also a lot of investment activity in and around Jakarta where a number of large industrial scale data centers are being developed by state-backed players such as Telkom, as well as private sector firms and investors. As reported by Antara News, Indonesia’s current data center capacity sits around 580 MW and the plan is to grow it to 1.3 GW in the near-term. Government data shows that investment in information services jumped from $967 million in 2023 to $3.4 billion in 2025 and it looks set to keep climbing.
Thailand is also now rushing to add more data centers, with several large industrial-scale projects in the pipeline. According to the Board of Investment, in 2025 they received $24 billion worth of applications across 151 projects in the digital industry, mainly data centers. Not all of these projects will be approved and become operational, but it again gives a sense of the speed and scale with which this industry is moving. Vietnam is following suit, with local media reporting that the government plans to reach 870 MW of data center capacity by 2030.
The trend is clear: data centers are beginning to pop up all around Southeast Asia, attracting billions of dollars in investment and uncorking a major construction boom. But a bigger, perhaps more fundamental, question is whether demand for digital services can justify these enormous outlays and the resources they will absorb. Investment is pouring into Southeast Asian digital infrastructure, with the expectation that businesses and consumers will spend billions of dollars on cloud computing, AI and other digital services in the years ahead.
This is not unique to Southeast Asia, of course. The same assumption about future demand has been driving eye-popping capex investment in data centers and cloud computing all around the world, raising similar questions. What we can say for sure is that the data center boom has reached the major economies of Southeast Asia. Whether these massive bets on future demand for digital services pays off is anybody’s guess. But considering the amounts of money involved, how this plays out is something we should all be watching very, very closely in the months and years ahead.

articles.title: Thailand’s Constitutional Court Dismisses Petition Seeking Annulment of General Election
articles.full_text:
The petition concerned the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballot papers, which some claimed could breach constitutional requirements for secret voting.
Thailand’s Constitutional Court yesterday dismissed a petition challenging the legality of the last general election, ​ruling that the ballot papers used did not undermine the confidentiality of the vote.
The ruling came in response to 22 complaints about the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballot papers in the February 8 election, which some claimed could breach constitutional requirements for secret voting, the Bangkok Post reported.
Nearly 38 ‌million Thais voted in the election, which was won decisively by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s Bhumjaithai Party. Bhumjaithai emerged from the polls with 192 of the 500 seats in the House of Representatives, and later formed a coalition government with a host of other parties, including the once-powerful Pheu Thai party (74 seats). The opposition People’s Party won 120 seats.
However, in the aftermath of the election, a host of complaints were submitted to the Election Commission (EC) for its adjudication, including complaints of alleged vote-buying, uncounted ballots, and other irregularities. While these were dismissed, it took the complaints about the use of barcodes and QR codes on ballots, which were ostensibly intended to counter fraud, more seriously.
In March, the Office of the Ombudsman ruled that there were sufficient grounds to question whether the EC and its leadership had acted in a way that contravened constitutional protections about voter confidentiality. If the Constitutional Court ruled that that the secrecy of the vote was compromised by the use of barcodes and QR codes, it had the power to annul the result of the election.
However, in its ruling yesterday, the Bangkok Post reported, the Constitutional Court said that that barcode and QR codes were “applied to prevent use of fake ballot papers and their cross-constituency use, and to control the number and printing of ballots.”
While the ballots contained information that could potentially be used to identify voters’ decisions, this information was only accessible if any outside party had access to used ballots, ballot stubs, and the lists of voters’ names – and then used mobile phones to scan the codes on all the documents. The fact that all three of these things were stored separately and were “sufficiently safe” from outside access, offered sufficient protection of the secrecy of the ballot, the Constitutional Court ruled.
Although the charter court endorsed the legality of coded ballots, it advised the EC not to use any codes that connected to the results in future.
The ruling averts ​this costly possibility of a new election – the Bangkok Post estimated that this would cost the Thai state upwards of 7 billion baht ($216 million) – and will no doubt come as a welcome relief for Anutin’s coalition government, especially given the Constitutional Court’s history of brash interventions in Thai politics.
Anutin has seen his approval ratings fall in recent months, due to rising living costs and political scandals involving corruption and the alleged rigging of the 2024 Senate election .
In a poll released on Sunday by the National Institute of Development Administration, only 13.8 percent of respondents chose Anutin as their preferred prime minister, down from 21.7 percent in June. Bhumjaithai’s rating declined from 17 percent to 12.1 percent over the same period, behind the People’s Party and the Pheu Thai Party.

articles.title: China’s Young Women Are Rewriting the Rules of Adulthood
articles.full_text:
Modernization has expanded women’s choices and made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.
In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children. 
Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?” 
Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021, allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities. 
Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood. 
Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.
Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer. 
Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman. 
Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her. 
The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy. 
She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms. 
For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage. 
Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken. 
The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present. 
Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default. 
That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem. 
“If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines. 
None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself.
Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home. 
Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined. 
The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held. 
Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i. 
Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. Her father countered instead with a story about a colleague’s child who’d quit an investment-banking job after three years, burned out. It was meant to be a cautionary tale about what a prestigious career actually costs. What her parents want for Iris is harder to define than pure career success. They want her to have a manageable life, to be somewhere stable, and eventually to come home. 
That expectation rarely arrives as a demand; it shows up in small comments instead. While Iris was in New York, her father compared New York’s infrastructure unfavorably to Shanghai’s. Her mother notes that Hangzhou “isn’t so bad” whenever Iris complains about where she’s living. When Iris mentions a hard week at work, the response is often some version of: why not just come home, find something stable? 
Nothing is framed as an ultimatum, and her parents insist the choice is hers, but the suggestions add up to a recognizable idea of what adulthood should eventually look like: stop drifting, settle, put down roots – back in China, of course. 
In China, the idea of settling down is hard to separate from marriage. For women in their 20s, stability tends to arrive bundled with questions about where they’ll live, whom they’ll marry, when they’ll start a family. Distance, Iris has found, gives her room to answer those questions on her own schedule. 
“In China, there is a pervasive pressure on women in their 20s to quickly find stability, buy an apartment, and marry,” she says. “In Hawai‘i, that marital clock simply vanishes.” 
That doesn’t mean the tension disappears, only that it changes shape. Iris is living inside one social world while carrying the expectations of another. The norms around her carry no real urgency about marrying or settling permanently. Her family’s expectations carry plenty. If she followed the culture in her new home, Iris risks feeling like she’s failing her family, but trying to import her family’s values wholesale doesn’t fit the life she’s actually building. 
“It’s a little like being caught in the middle,” she said. “The values your family brings with them don’t completely fit the society you’re living in, but you can’t just stop caring about what your family thinks either.” 
Iris still sometimes looks at friends her age who are marrying, buying homes, building linear careers, and wonders if she’s falling behind. Her own path has zigzagged instead: an exchange year in Japan, an unplanned application to NYU, offers turned down, a move to Hawai‘i with no five-year plan attached. But the uncertainty isn’t a side effect of her choices – it’s part of what she’s choosing.
articles.summary: Modernization has expanded women’s choices and made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.

articles.title: Trump Doesn’t Need to Be a Prop in Xi’s Political Show
articles.full_text:
Whether he means to or not, the U.S. president is feeding China’s active disinformation campaigns – especially on Taiwan.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during their summit at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
This September, I came across a post claiming that Hillary Clinton, the former U.S. senator and secretary of state, had urged Taiwan to surrender. With tens of thousands of likes and thousands of shares, the clip was spreading fast through Taiwan’s Chinese-language social media. Something felt off, so I checked. The truth was revealing. 
On September 10, the former U.S. secretary of state had appeared on “Morning Joe,” the MS NOW program’s September 11 anniversary special, to discuss U.S. President Donald Trump’s national security strategy. Iran, she said, backed by China and Russia, was deftly draining the United States’ capacity to defend its allies. 
Here’s what Clinton actually said (starting about 15 minutes into the interview): “We have to look at our potential dangers, especially what Xi is thinking, that they can’t defend anybody anymore, because they don’t have the capacity to defend. Maybe we can coerce Taiwan into just giving up because there’s not going to be any support.” 
She was describing what she believed Xi Jinping might now be calculating – not making a call of her own. By the time it reached Taiwan, her words had been mistranslated and spliced into something else entirely: “Hillary Clinton urges Taiwan to abandon resistance to China.” 
I know this playbook well. For years, as a spokesperson for Taiwan’s Cabinet and the Presidential Office, intercepting disinformation like this consumed most of my working hours. It is not a footnote to how Taiwan defends itself; it is the front line. We have learned, often the hard way, that 21st-century warfare runs on two tracks at once: the physical battlefield, where force is threatened or used, and the cognitive one, where information is weaponized to reshape how an adversary thinks, what it values, and what it believes to be true. Ideally for the attacker, cognitive warfare undermines the target from within before a kinetic attack is even contemplated. 
In May, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested publicly that arms sales to Taiwan could be treated as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Beijing. Whatever his intent, the remark landed squarely inside a narrative Beijing has spent years constructing: that Taiwan is China’s internal affair, and that outside powers – namely, the United States – have no legitimate role to play. Since then, Trump’s words have been recycled as raw material for Chinese cognitive warfare, feeding a relentless undertow of narratives that “America will abandon Taiwan,” “American troops are pulling out,” and “resistance is futile.” 
As this happened, the U.S. government remained silent. The State Department’s Chinese-language spokesperson, asked directly about the arms package, declined to comment and referred reporters to the Department of Defense. White House officials, pressed by reporters, would only say that Trump would decide on the arms sale “soon.” 
Beijing has spent years trying to push the United States out of the Indo-Pacific, and especially the Taiwan Strait. China has now effectively shifted the burden of keeping the peace onto Washington’s shoulders. What alarms me is that the Trump administration appears willing to accept that framing, treating Taiwan’s defense as something to be traded away. I believe this is a serious miscalculation. 
Some will say Trump’s remark was just tactical posturing, not a genuine concession, and they may be right. But intent matters less than how Beijing hears it: ambiguity is interpreted as weakness. China’s playbook over the past decade shows that such statements are seized upon, amplified, and repeated until they harden into a settled narrative. Whether he meant it or not, Trump’s comment on arms sales compresses Taiwan’s room for defense while enlarging the stage for Beijing’s cognitive warfare, adding pressure across the Western Pacific. 
China’s cognitive warfare tied to Trump-Xi summits is a well-established fact. Timed to launch in lockstep with Beijing’s own messaging, they were built to do two things at once: sow doubt about the United States’ commitment, and paint Taiwan as the aggressor.

Xi is using the meeting to restage Beijing’s long-running “peace” narrative for three audiences at once: at home, to shore up his own standing; globally, to sell the line that Taiwan is part of China; and inside Taiwan itself, as a direct cognitive assault. Trump’s hesitation on arms sales, whether he intends it or not, has bolstered those propaganda campaigns.. 
To Beijing, the United States has never been a friend, only an adversary to be defeated. Watching the once mighty Soviet Union collapse in 1991 badly rattled the Communist Party. Party leaders are convinced that Moscow did not simply fail economically or politically; it was worn down by a deliberate U.S. ideological campaign that hollowed out Soviet identity until there was nothing left to hold the union together. 
Whether or not that account is correct, it is what Chinese strategists believe. That is why Beijing has spent the decades since the Cold War studying U.S. information warfare and folding cognitive operations into its own military doctrine as a weapon to be used at home to secure the party’s grip, and abroad to advance its interests. 
Xi is contending with mounting challenges to his authority at home. He needed a show that put him on equal footing with the president of the United States to rally support domestically and help secure his continued leadership at the Communist Party’s 21st National Congress in 2027. Trump just handed him exactly that. 
Chinese state media have spent this week hailing the summit as “the first head-of-state reception of its kind in 60 years,” a “milestone” that cast Xi as the anchor of stability in China-U.S. relations. A CCTV program portrayed him as a great power leader steering the relationship “onto the right course.”

The goal is to manufacture a specific kind of anxiety: that Taipei cannot protect its own people, and that Washington will not help. China’s goal is not simply to sway one election. It is to paralyze Taiwan’s democratic system and lower the future cost of trying to invade the country. 
Trump does not have to play the prop in Xi’s political show. He could be the lead in his own narrative. That would mean delivering the arms already promised to Taiwan without further delay and resisting the temptation to treat Taiwan’s defense as a bargaining chip in any deal with Beijing. It would mean recognizing that every ambiguous remark about Taiwan’s status is heard in Taipei or Beijing, where it translates as an opening that China will exploit.

articles.title: India’s Sheikh Hasina Dilemma
articles.full_text:
New Delhi’s difficult decision serves as a masterclass in how personal diplomacy can trap a major power.
Protesters stamp the face of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in a poster on a street in Dhaka, Bangladesh, August 3, 2024.
The mass street uprising that overthrew Bangladesh’s long-serving prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, in August 2024 did more than just reset the politics of a nation. It completely broke the security architecture of eastern South Asia. For 15 years, India’s foreign policy in its immediate neighborhood relied on a single, unwavering rule: keep Hasina stable, and India’s eastern border remains secure.
Today, that strategy has brought about a major crisis. Hasina is living in exile on Indian soil, while a newly elected government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) runs Dhaka. A Bangladeshi court has convicted Hasina in absentia for crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death, leading Dhaka to officially demand her extradition.
This situation creates a complex challenge for New Delhi, known as the “Hasina dilemma.” It is a problem that cannot be solved simply by picking a side. Instead, it serves as a masterclass in how personal diplomacy can trap a major power, leaving India with difficult arguments to balance as it navigates this regional crisis.
India’s dilemma is rooted in a fundamental rule of global statecraft: credibility. For over a decade, Hasina risked her own domestic popularity to fulfil India’s core national security demands. Her government cracked down heavily on anti-India insurgent groups that used to hide in Bangladesh, arresting their leaders and handing them over to New Delhi. She opened up crucial transit routes, allowing Indian cargo ships and trucks to cut through Bangladesh to reach India’s landlocked northeastern states.
If India gives in to Dhaka’s demands and extradites Hasina to face a death sentence, it sends a dangerous signal to other neighbors like Bhutan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka: India will abandon its closest partners if the political winds change.
However, keeping Hasina protected inside India comes at an equally high cost. It provides permanent fuel for anti-India sentiment within Bangladesh’s civil society. The longer India acts as her shield, the easier it is for the BNP government to label New Delhi as an enemy of Bangladesh’s democracy. This anger puts India’s vital trade links and transit corridors at immediate risk of being shut down by a hostile public.
The strain on the relationship is no longer just quiet, back-channel friction; it has broken out into visible diplomatic boycotts. Rahman’s recent decision to skip the high-profile BRICS Summit hosted by India in New Delhi served as a clear example of this shift.
Dhaka viewed the invitation to the summit – extended to Rahman as the chair of a regional group (BIMSTEC) rather than as a direct, standalone invite to the premier – as a deliberate diplomatic snub by India. In retaliation, Rahman refused to travel to New Delhi altogether.
Instead, Rahman deliberately focused his diplomatic efforts elsewhere: a high-profile trip to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where he held a sideline meeting with the Pakistani leadership. At the same time, Rahman’s administration deepened talks with Beijing over major infrastructure loans.
By refusing a standalone visit to New Delhi, Rahman is sending a clear message: The days of Bangladesh automatically aligning with India’s foreign policy goals are over. Dhaka is demonstrating that it is fully willing to use its strategic geography to balance India’s influence, using closer ties with Islamabad and Beijing as leverage to show that Bangladesh is no longer dependent on New Delhi’s approval.
The Hasina Dilemma serves as a systemic warning to foreign policy planners worldwide: never mistake a single political leader for an entire country.
For 15 years, India’s Ministry of External Affairs operated under the assumption that keeping Hasina happy was equivalent to keeping Bangladesh stable. New Delhi looked the other way during consecutive, highly controversial Bangladeshi elections, prioritizing immediate border security over the growing domestic anger building up against her regime.
By tying its national interests so tightly to one person, India failed to build deep institutional relationships with Bangladesh’s opposition parties, its student movements, and its wider civil society.
Now that Hasina has fallen, India faces a significant penalty for this policy. The new leadership in Dhaka views almost every regular, technical bilateral issue – from regular border management to daily electricity grid sharing – through a lens of deep suspicion. Because India did not engage with the broader political spectrum when it had the chance, it must now build diplomatic capital from scratch with a suspicious administration, all while dealing with the political liability of hosting the former leader.
The relationship between India and Bangladesh cannot remain frozen in this defensive stance forever. Bangladesh relies heavily on India for daily essential food imports, medical tourism, and electricity. Conversely, India requires a cooperative Dhaka to ensure its northeastern states do not become cut off or vulnerable to security threats.
Signs of a realistic compromise are slowly beginning to show. Recognizing the danger of a complete breakdown in relations, India’s diplomats have adopted a quiet, disciplined approach, consistently stating their desire for a “constructive and forward-looking relations” with the new government. This back-channel diplomacy has successfully defused the initial freeze, setting up an official state visit for Rahman to New Delhi in late November or early December 2026.
To make this upcoming visit a success and move past the crisis, both nations must cooperate on a silent, two-part strategy.
First, find a third country willing to provide permanent asylum to Sheikh Hasina. India must quietly work to relocate Hasina to a secure country outside South Asia, such as in the Middle East or parts of Europe. This move would allow Dhaka to claim a political victory to its domestic voters while sparing India the immense loss of face that would come from direct extradition.
Second, India and Bangladesh must shift to transactional institutionalism. Both capitals must agree to treat critical issues – like the upcoming December 2026 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty deadline – as technical, non-negotiable economic necessities rather than emotional political weapons.
The Hasina Dilemma proves that in modern geopolitics, yesterday’s absolute stability can easily become tomorrow’s greatest strategic trap. Bangladesh-India relations will likely never return to the close, personal alliance of the past decade. The relationship has permanently shifted into a cooler, more transactional reality.
Even so, if both New Delhi and Dhaka can successfully separate their internal political speeches from their shared geographic realities, they can prevent the presence of a single deposed leader from turning a temporary diplomatic crisis into a long-term regional disaster.

articles.title: Is AUKUS Too Big to Fail?
articles.full_text:
The AUKUS partnership survived the Trump transition, and for Canberra it may be too big a deal to ever let fail.
Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS Minnesota (SSN 783) prepares to moor alongside submarine tender USS Emory S. Land (AS 39) during a scheduled port visit in Darwin, Northern Territory, Australia, March 27, 2025.
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics podcast, hosts Ankit Panda and Katie Putz mark the fifth anniversary of the AUKUS partnership with a discussion of the trilateral security agreement between Australia, the U.K., and the U.S., breaking down its significance, concerns regarding its sustainability amid a changing political landscape, the challenges faced by the U.S. submarine industrial base, and the implications of the partnership in the context of rising tensions with China. 
For more, check out our recent video explainer, featuring Dr. Euan Graham, further exploring the AUKUS partnership.
