articles.title: Options for the Royal Brunei Air Force’s Fast-jet Decision
articles.full_text:
One important mantra for the RBAirF: Don’t try to run before you can walk.
An FA-50 arrives in the Philippines for induction in the Philippine Air Force, June 1, 2017.
The Royal Brunei Air Force (RBAirF), which turned 60 in June, finds itself in a rapidly changing geostrategic environment, characterized by conflict and instability. Brunei is unlikely to suffer outright military aggression but could face spillover effects of increased super power confrontation in the region. 
Brunei’s recent defense white paper identified major power rivalry, regional and global conflicts, radicalization, and rapidly advancing disruptive technologies as sources of concern. It also laid out a path to secure national sovereignty and territorial integrity. The RBAirF is actively looking to expand its means to do so, including with plans to acquire medium-range ground-based air defense systems and fast-jet combat aircraft. 
Currently, the RBAirF operates a small fleet of modern turboprop-powered fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. In May, Brunei took delivery of the last two CASA (Airbus) C295W medium-airlift aircraft, first ordered in 2022. The aircraft replaced older C235 aircraft in the No. 15 Squadron in territorial and maritime surveillance, airlift, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions. 
For rotary-wing tactical airlift, search and rescue, and combat air support (CAS), the RBAirF operates a fleet of 12 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters and a handful of ageing BO105 helicopters. The latter is slated to be replaced by six Airbus H145M multirole helicopters. 
Finally, for basic flight training, the RBAirF flies four Pilatus PC-7 Mk.II turboprop aircraft. The aircraft were put into service in 1997, which makes them among the oldest aircraft in Bruneian service and in dire need for replacement.
To meet the air force’s mission – “to deliver responsive air power in securing Brunei Darussalam’s territorial integrity and national interests” – amid a changing security environment, more capable combat aircraft are also needed urgently. 
As the RBAirF considers the acquisition of a squadron of fast-jet combat aircraft, original equipment manufacturers (OEM) are lining up to offer their fighters to Brunei Darussalam. 
Options like the Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Viper offer a leap in capability for the RBAirF and come with closer ties with the U.S. defense industry and Washington D.C. However, the F-16 or an equivalent is not the best solution for the RBAirF as it seeks to enter fast-jet operations. Any decision regarding the RBAirF’s future combat aircraft should go beyond simple fighter comparisons and consider the air force’s broader requirements across its stated roles. 
Entering fast-jet operations also poses new training demands for the air force. Brunei will need a revised flight training syllabus and modern training aircraft to ready its future generation of pilots. 
Brunei could consider adopting the Singapore model by dispatching pilots to another country for advanced jet training (Phase 3-4), or join international advanced military flight training courses in Italy or Canada, while maintaining the elementary and basic training (Phase 1-2) at home.
Alternatively, the RBAirF could acquire the Embraer A-29 or Textron Aviation T-6 Texan II turboprop trainers to replace the aging PC-7 Mk. II fleet to meet its own advanced training (Phase 3) demands. 
Some air forces like Switzerland, for example, employ modern turboprop aircraft to fulfill their pilot training needs entirely (Phase 2-4), enabling pilots to transition from turboprop aircraft directly to jet combat aircraft. 
Moreover, both Embraer and Textron offer missionized and armed variants of their aircraft, which would offer Brunei an affordable light combat aircraft capability. The A-29 and AT-6 can be equipped with advanced electro-optical and infrared search and track, and laser track sensors, gun and rocket pods, and a variety of precision-guided munitions.
Critically, this would allow the RBAirF to meet many of its CAS, counterinsurgency (COIN), combat search and rescue, airborne forward air controller, armed reconnaissance, helicopter escort, and border and maritime surveillance patrol missions assigned to it with greater efficiency and capability than is possible today. 
Therefore, the two types offer substantial value at low cost. They would help support the Bruneian ground forces and navy, and other government agencies, and offer major savings that come from maintenance, operational, and training synergies of operating a common platform that meets the RBAirF’s basic military flight training requirements while fulfilling many of its lower end combat needs. 
To effectively protect Brunei’s airspace against intruders and assist in land and maritime border surveillance, rapid response (i.e., Quick Reaction Alert or QRA) is of essence. 
Neither the current turboprop aircraft or helicopters, nor turboprop light combat aircraft, can effectively intercept fast-moving and high-flying intruders near Bruneian sovereign airspace or above the exclusive economic zone. Therefore, the RBAirF requirement for fast jet combat aircraft is understandable. 
To meet the requirement, Brunei should consider acquiring modern multirole jet-trainer aircraft and their light combat aircraft variants, which could also fulfill the majority of the air force’s border protection and combat requirements. 
Good candidates to fill this role include, for example, the Leonardo M346F Block 20 and the Korean Aerospace Industries (KAI) TA/FA-50 Block 70 advanced jet trainer and light combat aircraft from Italy and South Korea respectively. Like the previously discussed turboprop options, Leonardo and KAI aircraft offer many synergies like in maintenance, training, and operations. 
The M346F Block 20 is a missionized advanced jet trainer, which is equipped with a modern active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, advanced cockpit with large-area display, and a helmet-mounted sight, datalink, targeting pod, short- and medium-range air-to-air missiles and a range of precision-guided air-to-ground and antiship weapons. 
Similarly, the latest FA-50 versions, such as the FA-50M and FA-50 Block 70 destined for Malaysia and the Philippines respectively, are fitted with an AESA radar, a targeting pod, a datalink, and a range of air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons.
Critically, the AESA radar, targeting pod, datalink, and the ability to carry both within-visual-range and beyond-visual-range missiles, enable the aircraft to take up the essential QRA and combat air patrol duties and respond to any airspace violations with force, if needed. 
The FA-50 holds an important advantage over the M346 in this regard. It can use its afterburning F404 powerplant to accelerate to a supersonic speed and reach the farthest reaches of Brunei’s EEZ faster than what is possible with the subsonic Italian aircraft. 
Besides their light combat aircraft attributes, both types were originally designed as advanced jet trainers to meet the common Phase 3 training requirements. The addition of a radar, fire-control computer and associated data bus, hardpoints, and weapons have enabled the use of the aircraft in lead-in fighter training (Phase 4) as well. 
In addition, both aircraft are equipped with large-area displays, helmet-mounted sights, and Virtual, Live, and Constructive (VLC) training aids, which promise to transform jet training in the coming years. The use of VLC allows air forces to achieve many previously difficult to resource training, such as large-force operations or weapons deployment at a significantly lower cost. 
For example, VLC can emulate a fire-control radar and simulate a beyond-visual-range missile engagement with all associated target and missile-launch symbology and cues projected on the displays and the helmet. Air forces can dispatch a pair of aircraft into air (“live”) while other trainees may join the same mission in simulators (“virtual”), while facing virtual enemy aircraft (“constructive”) – all linked to the same VLC environment.
Moreover, due to the rapid technological change and observations drawn from conflicts around the world, one-way attack drones (OWAD) have become a prominent aerial threat that requires solutions from air forces and the industry. 
Understanding this demand, OEMs like Embraer, Textron, and Leonardo market their aircraft as cost-effective counter-OWAD platforms, equipped with AESA radar and/or targeting pods, datalink, gun pods, short-range air-to-air missiles, and semi-active laser-guided rockets to address the threat.
articles.summary: One important mantra for the RBAirF: Don’t try to run before you can walk.

articles.title: Europe’s Read of the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
Decisions taken in Washington and Beijing increasingly shape European trade, technology, energy, and security.
U.S. President Trump delivers remarks to the press ahead of a summit meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
The summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping achieved one central objective: stabilization. It did not resolve the China-U.S. rivalry but helped contain it, by restoring a more predictable framework for managing tensions over trade, technology, and geopolitics. 
Its main concrete outcome was modest: a two-month extension, until January 2027, of the trade truce first agreed after the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan a year ago, when Washington lowered tariffs and Beijing suspended export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals.
The two sides also activated the China-U.S. Boards of Trade and Investment and mutual support for each other’s G20 and APEC presidencies. The message is clear: not genuine rapprochement, but more disciplined management of strategic competition. 
Yet the summit’s most consequential exchanges may have taken place behind closed doors over Iran. The public readout was brief, but Trump pressed Xi over Chinese support for Tehran, while both leaders publicly agreed that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
For the world’s two largest economies, which together account for nearly half of global economic output, de-escalation makes strategic sense, though for different reasons. Both sides would like to use a period of relative stability to buy time to reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen resilience, and recalibrate economic dependencies. 
Diplomatically, both leaders are also playing to domestic audiences. Trump is seeking tangible economic gains, from agricultural purchases to aircraft orders, consistent with his long-standing focus on reducing the U.S. trade deficit and addressing structural imbalances that have weakened American manufacturing. Xi, meanwhile, wants to show that Washington is treating China as an equal, while easing the economic pressure Washington has steadily increased toward Chinese companies. For Beijing, stability is economic as well as diplomatic: détente buys time to support a weak domestic economy increasingly reliant on external demand as consumption at home remains subdued.
The European Union was another important audience for the summit. Decisions taken in Washington and Beijing increasingly shape European trade, technology, energy, and security.
First, Brussels and major European capitals have a strong interest in stable China-U.S. relations, particularly at a time when instability in the Middle East is generating mounting economic pressures on Europe through higher energy costs, disrupted trade routes, inflationary pressures, and weaker industrial competitiveness.
Second, Europe fears becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition. Washington holds technological leverage; Beijing controls minerals and key manufacturing supply chains. Europe remains exposed to both. The question is whether the EU can turn its own economic weight into strategic agency rather than simply absorb the consequences of decisions taken elsewhere.
Consider trade relations. When China-U.S. trade tensions intensify, Chinese goods shut out of the American market are increasingly redirected toward Europe, raising fears of a deeper China shock. The automotive sector is already reshaping European perceptions of China, but the pressure extend well beyond card. The question is how many other industries will follow.

At the same time, any China-U.S. managed trade arrangement that redirects Chinese purchases toward American goods could come at the expense of European exporters. Europe therefore faces pressure in both directions, from trade diversion when tensions rise and from preferential bilateral deals when they ease. On the other side, if China-U.S. relations stabilize, Beijing has less incentive to make concessions to Brussels. Either way, Europe risks becoming the adjustment variable in China-U.S. competition: absorbing displaced Chinese production while bilateral deals between Washington and Beijing are struck largely over its head.

The recent China-U.S. summit produced no major new breakthrough, only an agreement to keep working on shortages and shipment levels.

There is still a risk that a bilateral China-U.S. accommodation could improve supply security for American companies without resolving Europe’s exposure. In response, Brussels is increasingly aligning with U.S.-led initiatives, such as Pax Silica, and its own Critical Raw Materials Act to diversify supply chains, though reducing dependence on China will require years of investment, industrial capacity building, and transatlantic coordination.

Disputes over advanced chip exports remain unresolved. Beijing has an interest in buying time to reduce its dependence on U.S. technology, without the added burden of new tariffs and restrictions on Chinese companies. 
For the EU, the risk is that the rules of AI race are increasingly shaped in a China-U.S. channel where Brussels has little influence. In the meantime, Europe remains heavily reliant on American processors and cloud providers and Chinese supply chains. The EU produces less than 10 percent of global semiconductors. Brussels is responding with its Technology Sovereignty Package paired with the Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act that aim to triple European data center capacity within five to seven years. Both acts are still proposals, however, with binding law months or possibly years away.

The European Union has considerable leverage of its own, through its market, regulatory power, trade instruments, and industrial base. The question is whether is prepared and unified to use that leverage with China. 
That is also why transatlantic coordination matters. Beijing benefits when U.S. and European positions diverge, while Washington has a clear interest in closer European alignment with its economic security approach. Europe’s strategic challenge is to avoid becoming merely the arena in which China-U.S. competition plays out and instead use its own agency to shape the terms of that competition.

articles.title: Lee Asks Trump to Help Revive North Korea Talks During New York Trip
articles.full_text:
During a Lee-Trump meeting at the U.N. General Assembly, Seoul said the U.S. president reaffirmed his willingness to talk with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung meets with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung asked U.S. President Donald Trump to help restart talks between the United States and North Korea in an unannounced meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, according to the Blue House, the presidential office of South Korea. The Blue House also said that Trump reaffirmed his willingness to engage with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The talks were arranged at the last minute. In the 30-minute meeting. Lee asked Trump to create a breakthrough amid almost no direct contact between the two Koreas. The two leaders also agreed to communicate closely as “peacemakers and pacemakers,” according to the Blue House. 
Trump has been courting Kim since August, when he scaled back a major joint military exercise with South Korea. A day later, he said Kim had responded to his request for dialogue, calling the exchange very positive without offering details. Trump has since signaled he hopes to meet Kim before the end of the year – possibly during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this November. 
Yet North Korea denied any direct contact in a statement by Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un. She described the relationship between the two leaders as “excellent” while insisting that Washington had not changed its hostile policy. She also said North Korea was not impressed by the reduction in scale of the South Korea-U.S. joint exercises, calling it “unworthy of comment.”
Lee had made the case for reopening dialogue earlier on September 22 in an address to the General Assembly. In the speech, Lee said he hoped to see the long-suspended dialogue between North Korea and the United States resume without delay. He also added that his administration would lay the groundwork for talks among the parties aimed at formally ending the Korean War.
On North Korean weapons, Lee outlined a sequence that would begin with a halt to further advances in North Korean nuclear and missile capabilities. Then reductions would follow over the medium term, with the ultimate goal of a Korean Peninsula free of nuclear weapons. Lee credited Trump with creating a hard-won opportunity for change and pledged to act as a “pacemaker” for peace.
The speech came a day after the foreign ministers of South Korea, the U.S., and Japan reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea in a joint statement issued on the sidelines of the same General Assembly session. The statement also urged Pyongyang to return to talks. 
North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui denounced the joint statement on September 24, declaring in a message carried by state media that the will of her country to keep nuclear weapons through all ages was “irreversible.”
Beyond North Korea, in their brief meeting Lee and Trump took up alliance issues such as nuclear-powered submarines and the transfer of wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the U.S. Rights to enrich uranium and reprocess spent nuclear fuel, along with shipbuilding cooperation, also came up. Both leaders also welcomed progress on investment projects between the two countries. The Industry Ministry had briefed lawmakers on a $22.3 billion gas-fired power plant in Texas, which Seoul confirmed as the first project under a $200 billion strategic investment package. Under the trade deal, South Korea has pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States, including $150 billion set aside for shipbuilding.
While in New York, Lee also met U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to review Korean Peninsula issues and cooperation between South Korea and the United Nations. In a separate meeting, he held talks with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on energy cooperation amid disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz. 
On September 23, Lee addressed the Korea Investment Summit in New York. He pledged to double semiconductor production capacity within five years and pointed to the shipbuilding cooperation covered in his meeting with Trump the day before.
Meanwhile, North Korea has said it tested a new weapon on September 20. That day, the South Korean military detected two short-range ballistic missile launches and assessed their flight distances at about 450 and 600 kilometers. Photos released by North Korea, however, showed a flight distance of 908.2 kilometers. 
The North Korean delegation skipped the General Assembly address delivered by Lee. Two North Korean diplomats had attended the speech given by Trump earlier that day.
The U.N. General Assembly also overlapped with a summit between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, during the first visit to the U.S. capital by Xi in more than a decade. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, to January 10. The White House later said China and the United States had reached consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction.
Each side also referred to the Korean Peninsula in its account of the talks. According to Washington, the two leaders discussed global concerns including Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Chinese state media reported that the leaders exchanged views on the Korean Peninsula, the Middle East, and the war in Ukraine. Neither side gave details of what was said about North Korea. 
After his trip to New York, Lee paid a state visit to Mexico. Lee and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum adopted a joint action plan for 2026 to 2030 and signed 17 cooperation documents covering areas from trade and critical minerals to aerospace and defense.

articles.title: The Trump-Xi Summit Is Over, But Taiwan Is Still Bracing for the Fallout
articles.full_text:
Given what happened in May, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended.
U.S. President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping of China arrive via the Cross Hall to a State Arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House, Sep.24, 2026.
The latest meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping led to much anxiety in Taiwan, with fears that Trump could potentially throw Taiwan under the bus in the course of negotiations with Xi. The two leaders agreed to dialogue on AI, as well as tariff reductions on $30 billion in “non-sensitive goods” going both ways. Even so, readouts between the two sides differed as to what was agreed to be purchased, and any discussion of semiconductors, chips, and export controls was not mentioned. 
Besides trade deals, there have been few concrete outcomes from the meeting to date, and the two leaders initially remained silent when asked by reporters if Taiwan featured in their summit. Trump later denied that Taiwan was discussed at length, then stated that he and Xi “didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”
Other reports suggest that Xi tried press Trump to curtail support for Taiwan, and accept Beijing’s framing on Taiwan. Chinese state-run media quoted Xi as stating during the meeting: “I hope that the United States adheres to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handles the Taiwan issue prudently.” 
In particular, ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, international media reporting suggested that Xi would try to convince Trump to cut weapons sales to Taiwan. Although the Trump administration approved $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan last December, the Trump administration has yet to approve a further $14 billion package. 
It was generally understood that Trump would not approve the arms sale ahead of his meeting with Xi, in order to ensure that the talks went smoothly. For its part, the Taiwanese government has attempted to reassure the public that ties with the United States are stable, and reiterated that U.S. policy on Taiwan has not changed after the summit. Nevertheless, the real question will be whether Trump reveals any unexpected curveballs for Taiwan after the meeting itself. 
If so, this would follow the precedent set by Trump after his meeting with Xi in May 2026 in Beijing. Little happened during the meeting itself, which was mostly a non-event. In May, as with this latest summit, Trump initially declined to answer questions on Taiwan from reporters. The readouts of the May 2026 meeting differed between the United States and China, with the U.S. denying that Taiwan had come up at all, while China claimed that it had been discussed. As if to forestall a potential shift in position by Trump,  U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio emphasized during the May trip that U.S. policy on Taiwan was unchanged in an interview with NBC. 
During an interview with Fox News shortly after his return from China, however, Trump seemed to hit out at Taiwan, stating that he was “not looking to have somebody go independent,” and that Taiwan needed “cool down a bit.” Trump then moved on to attack Taiwan with accusations that it had stolen the U.S. semiconductor industry, while calling on semiconductor companies to move back to the United States. 
Most alarming of all, Trump cast doubt on U.S. commitment to Taiwan as a whole, while suggesting that the Taiwan-U.S. relationship was mostly transactional. In particular, Trump suggested that arms sales to Taiwan were up for negotiation, and that this made for a “good bargaining chip” in talks with China. 
Such comments provoked alarm in Taiwan, seeing as this contravenes U.S. commitments to provide weapons to Taiwan dating back to the Reagan-era Three Assurances. Trump also raised questions about whether the United States would intervene in the event of a conflict with China, stating that he did not think it was logical for American troops to “travel 9,500 miles to fight a war.”
Given that recent history, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended. 
Indeed, indications have since emerged that Trump offered to sell arms to China during his September meeting with Xi. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, stated that Trump made such comments to Xi in an interview with Fox News on September 27. Although Perdue also stated that U.S. policy remained unchanged on Taiwan, this was an unusual comment by Trump. The offer came only a few days after controversy erupted about F-35 parts that were mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, raising concerns about sensitive U.S. military technology ending up in Chinese hands. 
As such, while Taiwan may have breathed a sigh of relief that the September summit has not resulted in any overt shift in U.S. policy on Taiwan, what remains is to see whether Trump shifts later on. As some analysts have noted, Trump has already echoed Chinese language on Taiwan on numerous occasions in the past. And while some elements of his administration, such as Rubio, may emphasize that policy remains unchanged, this is not reassuring when Trump himself contradicts those statements.
It is still uncertain when further U.S. arms sales to Taiwan will be approved. Trump and Xi are set to meet two more times this year, in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, as well as at the G20 summit in December at the Trump National Doral Miami Golf Club in Florida. It is possible that Trump will hold off on arms sales until after these meetings, or until 2027. Trump’s decision whether to approve arms sales or not could also be impacted by the U.S. midterm elections in November. 
With the Trump administration holding off on approving arms sales to Taiwan, this may complicate the domestic debate on defense spending. In past years, the United States has sought to pressure Taiwan to increase defense spending to 5 percent or even 10 percent of GDP, with Trump himself suggesting that the U.S. should not defend Taiwan if Taiwan is not serious about its own defense. 
But at a time of stark partisanship, the Kuomintang (KMT) delayed for over 200 days on reviewing the central government budget, while enacting widespread cuts to government ministries it views as antagonistic. The delays impacted defense spending, as well as spending on Taiwan’s domestic drone program. Even so, the KMT suddenly reversed course in August to finally approve the budget, though it limited drone spending by passing it as part of the central government budget rather than as a special expenditure. 
Efforts by the United States to push Taiwan to increase defense spending are likely to ring hollow in Taiwan if Washington refuses to sell Taiwan arms. Likewise, comments by Trump will increase doubts about U.S. reliability as an ally in wartime – indeed, survey polling shows that skepticism about the U.S. is up across the board in Taiwan. (Such polling also shows an increase in the Taiwanese public’s willingness to fight – even without U.S. intervention.) Certainly, with the United States holding off on arms sales to Taiwan for so long, Trump suddenly offering to sell arms to China is not likely to reaffirm faith in the U.S. in Taiwan. 
Increased skepticism about U.S. reliability is likely to lead to efforts to shore up Taiwan’s domestic defense programs, which are not reliant on the mercurial nature of arms sales. Taiwan is especially likely to seek cooperation from non-U.S. partners on drone development, while positioning itself as an alternative to drone supply chains highly reliant on China. 
It can be expected that summits between Trump and Xi will fall into this familiar script going forward – even when the meetings themselves may result in little substance, the point is to see what occurs afterward, and how left-field comments or actions by Trump are perceived.

articles.title: Ismat Ara on India’s Crackdown on Love
articles.full_text:
Ara explains the insidious harm of the “love jihad” myth: “A deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to violently police.”
Love and marriage across religious and caste lines have always been frowned upon and forbidden in India. However, Hindu right-wing organizations have taken this to a new extreme by conjuring up a conspiracy theory they term “love jihad.” India is witnessing a systematic strategy being implemented by Hindutva activists to not just prevent Hindu women from marrying Muslim men but to malign the latter by ascribing to them sinister motives of enticing Hindu women with false promises of love and marriage for the sole purpose of converting them to Islam. Bharatiya Janata Party politicians have used the “love jihad” bogey to deepen Hindu anxieties and polarize society. BJP governments in several states have enacted anti-religious conversion laws. Meanwhile, right-wing goons have wreaked enormous havoc in the lives of young couples who dare to love across religious lines.
In her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love,” author Ismat Ara recounts the enormous stress and suffering that Hindu-Muslim couples experience. She draws attention to how the “love jihad” “myth” has come to “define an entire community.” In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara pointed out that while an interfaith relationship is a private matter between two people, “within the ‘love jihad’ narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.”
“Love jihad” is the idea that Muslim men are deliberately targeting Hindu women for relationships and marriage in order to convert them to Islam, and that this is part of a larger organized conspiracy. It is an elaborate example of political myth-making and what happens when paranoia about “Muslim danger” enters the mass psyche.
While doing fieldwork for my recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky,” what interested me was not only whether individual cases of deception or coercion exist — they can, as they do in any relationship — but how these individual cases are transformed into evidence of a larger, vast conspiracy, one that comes to define an entire community. The leap from “a Muslim man deceiving a woman” to “Muslim men are conducting an organized campaign against Hindu women to take over this country” is the crucial political leap. When it becomes part of a larger conspiracy, the myth then becomes powerful enough to shape families, communities, police action, and even public policy, acquiring a life of its own, with its own set of myths.
There have been cases such as the 2023 Purola episode in Uttarakhand, where an alleged attempt to abduct a 14-year-old girl was quickly branded as “love jihad,” triggering communal protests and the exodus of Muslim families. The case later collapsed in court, with the girl and her uncle contradicting the initial police version. The minor also told the court that police had tutored her to make allegations against the accused, who were subsequently acquitted.
Could you share with us an example of what an interfaith couple undergoes when they are accused of “love jihad”? 
Once people believe the myth of “love jihad,” real couples have to live with its consequences. One of the stories I reported from Uttar Pradesh is of a Hindu woman and a Muslim man who got married. After their nikah (wedding), when the couple went to the district magistrate’s office for their marriage registration, the man was shot in the head by two unidentified assailants right outside the government office in broad daylight. The couple wanted to register their marriage, make it official so no harm could touch them. But the woman saw her husband die before her eyes, minutes before that.
What made the story particularly chilling is the context. The couple had received warnings for weeks and months from local right-wing outfits and people opposed to the relationship and believed that once they had an official stamp from the government, no harm could touch their marriage. So, what began as a deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to intervene in, threaten, and violently police.
In another example, from Gujarat, a state still scarred by the communal violence of 2002, a stamp vendor who had sold the couple their marriage stamps went on to call the woman’s family to inform them of their daughter’s “misdoings,” escalating the tension further.
In your book, you argue that “love jihad” is all about controlling women. Could you explain how?
One of the book’s main premises is that this is ultimately about controlling women, and that control operates across communities, although in very different ways. When a Hindu woman is told that she cannot choose her own partner because he belongs to another faith, her agency is being taken away. She is often treated as someone who has been deceived or brainwashed rather than as an adult capable of making a decision. But I also looked at Muslim women in the book. There is a case of a Muslim woman whose parents oppose her marriage because the man she has chosen was not just Hindu, but also belonged to a lower caste. The woman was told by her family that they might have considered a Hindu man — but only if he was upper caste. So, the policing of women’s choices isn’t confined to one community.
It’s an old story of women’s choices being made to represent the honor of an entire community, but what is distinctive about the “love jihad” campaign specifically is the way the Hindu woman has increasingly been made into a symbol, used as a tool, almost as the keeper of her entire community’s honor, purity, and demographic future. Her personal choices are seen as a collective threat. She is considered incapable of making her own decision, but in reality, her decision is powerful enough to threaten the demographic future of an entire community.
Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes an individual’s freedom to choose whom they wish to marry. In reality, less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, so this has never been an easy choice. It has always meant navigating disapproving parents, nosy neighbors and hostile looks. But increasingly, crossing that boundary can also mean the police coming to your home. These single-digit marriages are framed as “dangerous” or as something that could alter India’s demography.
“Love jihad” is fundamentally a threat-based concept: it brings together anxieties around women, community honor and national security. But what about the real wars being fought by women? The opposite can be opportunity-based concepts, focusing on potential gains, growth, and positive outcomes rather than on “avoiding dangers or risks.” We must look at the basics that affect the majority of our country’s women, from the girl child being killed to girls not getting education or healthcare access.
Could you share with us how right-wing organizations mobilize and prevent interfaith marriages?
The “foot soldiers,” as well as organizations that work around “love jihad” cases, have multiple sources of information and multiple ways of mobilizing. Some maintain strong local networks; others are highly visible on the street, actively watching for such cases. In some places, they don’t even need to go looking. They have become such recognized “authorities” that people from neighboring areas approach them directly to report what they see as suspicious behavior, or word that a Muslim man is trying to “lure” a Hindu woman.
There are also rehabilitation programs aimed specifically at women, meant to remind them of their religious identity and, in the language of these organizations, to “correct” or undo the ideological influence they are believed to have absorbed from Muslim men. It is not one form of mobilization but many: surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which an interfaith relationship becomes something the wider community feels entitled to police.
The Special Marriage Act of 1954 was supposed to help interfaith couples marry. Why hasn’t it worked?
A law can create a legal route, but societal adoption of that route is equally important. The Special Marriage Act was meant to allow people of different faiths to marry without requiring either person to convert. But over the years, interfaith marriage has become increasingly politicized, particularly when it involves a Hindu woman and a Muslim man. The problem is that couples aren’t operating in a social vacuum. They have to navigate families, communities, local officials, and, increasingly now, political scrutiny. A legal provision cannot by itself remove the social stigma or the fear surrounding the choice. The Special Marriage Act exists, but the real question is whether people feel genuinely safe to use it. What do couples do when the law gives you a right, but the process through which you exercise that right can expose you to physical, mental, emotional and legal risks?
Allegations of “love jihad” are usually hurled at Muslim men marrying Hindu women. Are such allegations levelled against Muslim women marrying Hindu men?
Yes, there have been cases where Muslim women have faced similar allegations, particularly allegations that they were attempting to convert Hindu men through marriage. In Uttar Pradesh, for instance, there have been cases where criminal complaints under anti-conversion laws were filed against Muslim women and their male relatives, with families alleging that conversions were being orchestrated through the promise of marriage. In some cases, Muslim women have even been sent to custody in connection with such allegations. So, the idea of a Muslim woman being an agent of conversion is certainly present in some cases.
If religious conversions did not happen, would anxieties that fuel “love jihad” allegations reduce?
Conversion sits at the center of the “love jihad” narrative, but I don’t think its absence would make the deeper anxiety disappear. One thing that became clear to me while reporting these stories is that suspicion often exists even where no conversion has taken place at all. A Hindu woman simply being in a relationship with a Muslim man can be enough to trigger the allegation of “love jihad.” There has been no substantial body of cases establishing an organized “love jihad” conspiracy behind forced conversions. Individual cases of coercion or deception can occur, of course, and deserve to be investigated on their own merits, but that is a very different thing from proving a larger, organized conspiracy.
What happens, then, is that the political idea becomes much larger than the evidence behind it. I sometimes think of it like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’s monster: something that is created and then acquires a life of its own. The narrative begins to generate its own evidence. An interfaith relationship becomes suspicious because people have already been told what such a relationship means; the absence of conversion does not necessarily dispel the suspicion. So, conversion is important to the mythology, but it is not really the whole story. The deeper anxiety is about the crossing of community boundaries through intimacy and marriage. Who is allowed to love whom? What happens when a woman chooses a partner from another community? What religion will the children follow? Will the family retain its religious identity? And that is why I see “love jihad” as part of a larger politics of controlling women’s choices.
The policing of interfaith marriage exists across communities. Muslim women too can face enormous family and social pressure when they marry outside the community. But “love jihad” has given that anxiety a particularly powerful political vocabulary when the relationship is between a Hindu woman and a Muslim man.
The Christian Church in Kerala has also accused Muslims of “love jihad.” How similar is their campaign against interfaith marriage?
While there are similarities, there are also important differences. The similarity is in the underlying anxiety: the fear that women from one’s own religious community are being targeted by men from another community, and that such relationships could lead to conversion, loss of community identity, or demographic change. But the Christian discourse in Kerala has been more localized and has emerged from a very different social and political context, rooted largely in concerns within the Christian community about young women, interfaith relationships, and conversion.
The “love jihad” narrative in the wider Hindu nationalist discourse, on the other hand, has acquired a much larger political vocabulary. It has been linked not just to conversion and interfaith marriage, but also to concerns about demography, population growth, religious identity and, at times, national security. It has therefore travelled far beyond individual relationships and become part of a broader political narrative. These campaigns may emerge from different contexts, but they draw upon an older anxiety around women, sexuality and community boundaries.
So I would say the resemblance is real, but the scale, impact, context, and political consequences are different.
articles.summary: Ara explains the insidious harm of the “love jihad” myth: “A deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to violently police.”

articles.title: Why Pakistan Turned on the Taliban (and Vice Versa)
articles.full_text:
Why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé?
On the night of February 21, 2026 Pakistan launched air and missile strikes on three border provinces in Afghanistan. What was Pakistan bombing? Suspected camps of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – the TTP for short – and the Islamic State of Khorasan Province. 
The Taliban regime in Afghanistan retaliated by hitting Pakistani border posts. 
Pakistan then upped the ante. Its military launched Operation Ghazab Lil-Haq — which means Righteous Fury — against Afghanistan. 
“Our patience has now run out. Now it is open war between us,” Pakistan’s defense minister said on February 27. 
Pakistan and Afghanistan have engaged in numerous strikes and counter-strikes in the months since. While these have declined in frequency and magnitude, thanks to mediation efforts by China, the military strikes were still happening into September 2026. TTP attacks in Pakistan have also continued. 
Few would have expected Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to turn on each other. They had been close allies for over 30 years – through the Taliban’s entire existence. When the Taliban captured power in Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan celebrated. 
So why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé? Is there more to Pakistan’s military strikes on Afghanistan than taking out TTP camps? And can the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship be salvaged?

articles.title: Indonesia Finally Has Its Aircraft Carrier. Now Comes the Hard Part.
articles.full_text:
Following a controversial acquisition, the most pressing question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the vessel into a viable military asset.
The Italian aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, now the KRI Sriwijaya of the Indonesian Navy, steams through the Atlantic Ocean while participating in Majestic Eagle 2004, July 12, 2004.
Last year, reports surfaced that Indonesia was considering acquiring an aircraft carrier for the first time in its history. This prompted a heated debate over whether Indonesia truly needed an aircraft carrier. In an article published in The Diplomat, I argued that Indonesia didn’t need such an acquisition, at least for the time being, for a variety of reasons. The arrival of the KRI Sriwijaya, as the new vessel is known, thus marks the end of one discussion and the start of another. The key question now is whether Indonesia can turn the ship into a sustainable military capability.
On September 18, the aircraft carrier, formerly known as ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, arrived at Tanjung Priok Port in Jakarta. The ship was personally welcomed to port by the minister of defense, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and the chief of naval staff. A formal handover from the Italian Navy to the Indonesian Navy took place on September 24, at which the carrier was reflagged and christened with its new name,
The name chosen by the Indonesian government has important symbolic importance. Sriwijaya was a strong monarchy and a respected naval power in Sumatra from the 7th to the 13th centuries.
However, with the ship’s arrival, the most important question is whether and how Indonesia can convert the ship into a viable military asset?
Aircraft carriers are often associated with naval superiority. Their ability to carry and operate aircraft or helicopters from the sea provides flexibility in projecting power, extending a navy’s range of operations, while also offering strategic options that do not entirely depend on land-based airfields. Moreover, the possession of an aircraft carrier with its various strategic values also brings prestige.
However, an aircraft carrier is not an arms technology that can produce strategic effects independently. Like other conventional weapon technologies, the effectiveness of an aircraft carrier heavily relies on the supporting ecosystem that enables it to operate sustainably and safely. In general, aircraft carriers never sail independently. In operation, the aircraft carrier will be part of a carrier strike group (CSG), which usually consists of an aircraft carrier, a guided missile cruiser, anti-aircraft warships, and anti-submarine destroyers or frigates. In carrying out its operations, the aircraft carrier is also often escorted by attack submarines.
The ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was always escorted by other warships while still flying the Italian flag. For example, during the Passing Exercise in the Mediterranean Sea in 2020, Garibaldi was accompanied by at least two multirole frigates and one supply ship.
In a CSG, each element has a complementary function, ranging from air defense, anti-submarine warfare, protection of the aircraft carrier, logistics, to command and control. Therefore, the capabilities produced by the CSG are the result of the integration of various platforms, not merely a consequence of the presence of an aircraft carrier itself.
In the context of Indonesia, the issue of the availability of escort and support fleets for aircraft carrier operations becomes is a very important issue. Indonesia indeed now has its long-awaited carrier, but still lacks surface warships to form a CSG as commonly found in the United States or French navies. Referring to the Laboratorium Indonesia 2045 database, Indonesia still lacks 12 frigates and seven fast missile boats to fulfil the government’s Archipelagic Trident Shield defense posture goals. The same goes for the submarine fleet. Indonesia is recorded to still be short of at least eight submarines.
The government and the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) have indeed stated on several occasions that the presence of KRI Sriwijaya is not intended for expeditionary combat missions. They argue that the aircraft carrier will instead be prioritized for military operations other than war, specifically humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR). For instance, once operational, the government stated that KRI Sriwijaya would join other TNI forces to assist in handling the  ongoing forest fires in Kalimantan. In addition to HADR missions, the Indonesian Navy chief of staff has said that the carrier will be used for defense diplomacy activities, such as port visits.
At first glance, the government’s and TNI’s statement to prioritize HADR missions and defense diplomacy for KRI Sriwijaya sounds rational. Besides the fact that Indonesia’s military posture does not allow for offensive operations, this statement is also expected to prevent diplomatic tensions with other countries, especially in the region.
However, this again raises the question of whether Indonesia truly requires an aircraft carrier. HADR can be a relevant mission for KRI Sriwijaya, but the relevance of a mission does not automatically prove that the chosen platform is the most effective way to achieve that capability. To ensure that KRI Sriwijaya can fulfill its role, Indonesia must still build the right ecosystem around it. For example, if it is intended for HADR missions on land, then Indonesia must ensure the availability of adequate transport helicopters. If Indonesia does not invest in acquiring a sufficient number of transport helicopters, then the KRI Sriwijaya will only become a sitting duck in the middle of the Nusantara sea when a disaster occurs on land.
In other words, if Sriwijaya is to be used for HADR missions, the measure of its success should not stop at the ship’s ability to carry helicopters to disaster areas. A more important question is whether the entire ecosystem built around the ship produces HADR capabilities that are significantly higher than the simpler and more cost-effective alternatives. At this point, Indonesia needs to realistically define the capabilities that it actually wants to derive from Sriwijaya so that it can then build the appropriate ecosystem around it.

articles.title: The Islamabad Memorandum Returns to the Spotlight
articles.full_text:
For Pakistan, the coming days will test whether its mediation capacity can keep pace with a conflict that continues to expand in both geography and complexity.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (left) shakes hands with Iranian President Dr. Masoud Pezeshkian at their meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA meeting in New York, Sept. 24, 2026.
The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that Pakistan helped negotiate between Iran and the U.S. in June and which had largely dropped out of public discussion in recent months is back in the news again. The renewed attention on the MoU, however, does not necessarily indicate a clear pathway toward a lasting de-escalation of the conflict. Rather, it signals a new high level of endorsement since its signing in June.
The Pakistan-mediated 14-point interim understanding that Washington and Tehran endorsed was intended to halt the armed hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and create space for broader talks on nuclear and other issues. Its recent return to high-level conversations during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) summit in New York suggests that, despite repeated setbacks, the agreement still serves as the primary reference point for those seeking to prevent further escalation.
The latest references to the MoU emerged largely at meetings held on the sidelines of this year’s UNGA. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking after discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, stated that the entire Pakistani leadership remained united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts outlined in the Islamabad MoU. Pezeshkian, for his part, reaffirmed that the memorandum remained “totally acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward. These remarks, delivered after weeks of relative quiet, signaled that both sides of the original mediation still viewed the document as a viable baseline for de-escalation.
Chinese President Xi Jinping added further weight to the MoU during his state visit to the United States last week. In talks with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, Xi expressed support for the U.S. and Iran returning to the June deal that was meant to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also said that both parties should resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and reach a comprehensive agreement that included the nuclear issue.
Amid this renewed focus on the June agreement, President Xi’s intervention carried particular significance because it came amid broader discussions on global economic stability. The Chinese leader also noted that new economic and trade arrangements between Beijing and Washington represented positive news for the economies and peoples of both countries and for the world economy at large. By linking regional de-escalation to the condition of the global economy, Xi underscored that the prolonged crisis in West Asia carries costs that go far beyond the immediate theater of conflict.
While these high-level statements are important, developments on the ground indicate that negotiations have not gathered significant momentum. For instance, Iranian officials held three hours of talks with U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of UNGA. This was the first such contact since U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June to advance the memorandum. The meeting itself produced no public breakthrough, but its occurrence after months of silence suggested that channels remain open.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi injected urgency into these latest conversations by stating that if the necessary conditions were met, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. He emphasized that the actions required of the U.S. are already contained in the MoU and that the choice now resides with Washington.
Meanwhile, Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with some reports indicating that the U.S. is planning another round of attacks on Iran after the upcoming midterm elections. Meanwhile, Iranian officials appear to have ignored Trump’s rhetoric, saying that they are waiting for an official response from mediators on the proposals under discussion within the Islamabad framework.
For Pakistan, the renewed focus on the MoU offers another opportunity to press for de-escalation between Iran and the U.S., especially since the agreement now has Xi’s explicit backing.
However, the stakes for Islamabad have grown considerably since June. Pakistan is no longer focused solely on salvaging the original understanding. The country’s policymakers are simultaneously attempting to help ease tensions between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia as well as Iran and the U.S.
Last week, the military leadership from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan convened under the joint Makkah defense pact to discuss urgent steps in support of the Saudis amid Houthi attacks. The three countries resolved to accelerate military cooperation, with Islamabad and Riyadh separately committing to joint efforts to confront threats to Saudi territory. This expanded mediation portfolio has arguably stretched Pakistan’s diplomatic capacity at a time when the original Iran-U.S. conflict has only broadened in scope.
Moreover, there are additional risks which can complicate the picture. For instance, Trump has reportedly hinted at the possibility of renewed military action against Iran even as de-escalation talks continue. Tehran has responded with warnings of new military surprises should it come under attack. Iranian officials have also cautioned that any future confrontation could extend the conflict into the Arabian Sea.
It is pertinent to mention that Pakistan possesses no enforcement mechanism within the Islamabad MoU. The country’s influence rests solely on the goodwill of the primary parties and the diplomatic capital it has accumulated through mediation efforts. As the war continues to stretch and new fronts are opening, there is a growing risk that the original understanding may be overtaken by events, which could put additional pressure on Islamabad’s carefully cultivated role as a regional mediator.
The Islamabad MoU has arguably returned to the diplomatic conversations not because its implementation is imminent, but because it remains the only structured framework both sides have formally accepted as part of a de-escalation mechanism.
Whether that framework can still function as a roadmap depends less on statements delivered in New York or Washington and more on the willingness of Iran and the U.S. to translate words into actions on the ground.
